en: How do you fund art school in 1900s Iceland? Your shipmates **pass a hat round a freezing cod trawler**. Not a GoFundMe — an actual hat.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered out east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **"Jói í Geitavík."** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, the fishermen's union topped it up. **1911**: he tried **London** — the **Royal Academy slammed the door**. The rejection was the redirect: **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Home again he painted Iceland like no-one had — knelt over the **moss and lava three inches from his nose**, and swore he saw **elves and hidden folk** in the cracks. (In Iceland, that's not a diagnosis. That's a career.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: In **1968** he handed the city **a huge part of everything he owned** — the museum's Kjarval collection runs to **thousands of works** — and he died **owning almost nothing.** That grey block in Klambratún is **Kjarvalsstaðir**, Iceland's **first purpose-built art museum** (1973); since **1995** his face is on the **2,000-króna note** — the only cod fisherman ever **promoted to legal tender.**

en: How do you run Iceland's most famous brewery when beer is **illegal for 74 years**? Name it after a Viking — and brew beer that technically isn't beer.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Founded **17 April 1913** by **Tómas Tómasson** in two basement bedrooms of a rented Reykjavík house — at first just **1%-alcohol malt extract** — and named after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the warrior-poet who once rhymed his way off an executioner's block (the *Höfuðlausn*, "Head-Ransom") and could drink a whole hall under the table. Aspirational branding.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915) — so Tómas sails to **Copenhagen and Germany (1915–17) to learn brewing anyway**, training up for a product his own country just outlawed. Wine creeps back in **1922**, spirits in **1935**, but **beer stays illegal until 1989**. Beer alone, because it read as **Danish** — and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: So Ölgerðin cheats: brews **Egils Pilsner kept just under the legal 2.25%** — beer that technically wasn't beer. A loophole in a glass. (The orange **Appelsín**, drowned in malt every Christmas, came later — **1955**.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The irony peaks in **1926**: after a state visit from King **Christian X**, Ölgerðin wins the right to style itself the **"royal brewery"** — a Danish royal blessing, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Real beer returned **1 March 1989** — now **Bjórdagurinn, "Beer Day."** Egils didn't fight for shelf space; they already owned it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Most capitals get a grey, sad little river. Reykjavík's hands you **dinner, drinking water, electricity — and the country's first parliament.** Show-off.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of the only **capital-city rivers on Earth with a wild Atlantic salmon run**. About **2,500** shove upstream past the joggers every summer to spawn — and the city was so smitten it **bought the whole river in 1906**. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The **pure tap water** your hotel keeps bragging about? Springs in this same catchment, up by the lake **Elliðavatn** — the city first drew its drinking water here in **1909**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The lights? In **1921** they dammed it for **Elliðaárstöð** — **Reykjavík's** first power station and **Iceland's second** hydro plant, switched on by King **Christian X** in person on **27 June 1921** and still running a century later.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits the ground identified since **1841** as the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, held by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. **Ari fróði** put that þing on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, fourteen kilometres away, and nobody has ever closed the gap. The old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it. (More on parliaments shortly.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The heat, too. Reykjavík's hot water did not start with volcanoes, it started **inside the city** — **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells are still working, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** (Yes, the ground gets a lie-down.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: There is even a chemical reason your shower behaves oddly here: water from the **Laugarnes** wells is **high in silica**, which deposits on taps and tiles as it cools, while water from **Nesjavellir and Hellisheiði** is heated groundwater and **low in silica.** Same tap, different geology.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: That ridge isn't a mountain — it's a **volcanic range** with **11 ice ages** stacked inside it. Reykjavík's **weather forecast, written in stone** — and unlike the app, it's never wrong.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: **Esja** rose between **3.2 and 1.8 million years ago**, west end oldest — it's been weathering longer than humans have existed, and it isn't one mountain but a whole **volcanic range**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: The stripes are climate you can read from your seat: **dark basalt** flowed in **warm, ice-free** spells and cooled in peace; **pale móberg** (tuff) is lava that picked a fight with a glacier and lost — shattered to rubble under the ice.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: Count the bands and you're counting cold snaps: geologists read **at least 11 separate ice ages** in there. Makes this winter look like a warm-up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja

en: True summit is **Hábunga (914 m)** — which almost nobody bothers with. The crowd-pleaser is **Þverfellshorn (~780 m)**, where a boulder called **Steinn**, about **200 m below the top**, is the official "close enough, take the selfie" turnaround. Touch the rock, you climbed Esja. We don't ask questions.

en: The Parliament Before the Parliament
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. The original ran over there on Kjalarnes — set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — son of **Ingólfur Arnarson**, Iceland's first settler — held the **Kjalarnesþing** before the national **Alþingi of 930**. Our only near-contemporary source is **Ari fróði**, writing around **1122–33**: *"en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi"* — before that, the þing was on Kjalarnes. Tradition even credits Þorsteinn with **consecrating** that later national parliament — so the founder's son didn't just build the prototype, he blessed the sequel.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Here's the catch: nobody has ever found it on Kjalarnes.** **Jónas Hallgrímsson** went looking in **1841**, examined **Leiðvöllur** on the farm **Esjuberg**, and decided it was a footpath. The national register still lists that spot as *sést ekki* — nothing to see. What he found instead was **14 km away, at Þingnes on Elliðavatn**: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring 43 feet across** with a heap of stones in the middle. He proposed that was the Kjalarnesþing, and in **1930** the state made it official — the protection order calls Þingnes *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*. **Thirteen ruins are protected there today**, last surveyed in **June 2025**. The join between Ari's Kjalarnes and Jónas's Þingnes has **never been proven** — so Iceland's first parliament is a place we can name and can't quite find.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: To write proper laws, the chieftains didn't reinvent the wheel — they sent one man, **Úlfljótr**, to **Norway for three years** to study the **Gulating law** and adapt it for home. He came back with **Úlfljótur's Law**, Iceland's **first law code** — but with one radical twist the Norwegians didn't have: a parliament with **no king**. That part was all theirs.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: Nothing was written down — Iceland had no writing worth the name — so **Úlfljótur carried the whole code home inside his head.** He was sent **shortly before 930** and spent **three winters** in Norway, landing home in time for the founding of the **Alþingi in 930**. What he recited is **Úlfljótslög**, the oldest law this country has. Úlfljótur supplied the text. Þingvellir only supplied the venue.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Iceland's first legal draftsman has a lake, a farm and a church carrying his name** — **Úlfljótsvatn**, Úlfljótur's water — and almost nobody stops at any of the three. (The church is the fun one: open a guidebook and it was built in **1914**, open the national heritage register and it was built in **1863**, by **Eyjólfur Þorvarðsson**, *forsmiður frá Bakka*. When two dates disagree, take the one with the carpenter in it.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The famous line **"með lögum skal land byggja"** — with laws shall the land be built — gets hung round Úlfljótur's neck constantly, and **he almost certainly never said it.** It arrives in Iceland with **Járnsíða**, a Norwegian king's code imposed between **1271 and 1274**, in the fuller form **"með lögum skal land vort byggja en eigi með ólögum eyða"**, and the phrasing traces back to Norway's **Frostaþingslög**. That makes it about **three hundred and fifty years too young** to be his.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **The silver (from Egil's saga):** in old age the warrior-poet **Egill Skallagrímsson** — sitting on two chests of silver gifted by **King Æthelstan of England** (the same Egill the brewery back in town is named after) — slipped off during the Alþingi with the silver, a horse and two slaves. The horse came back. Egill came back. The slaves and the silver didn't — he killed them to keep the spot secret. A thousand years of treasure hunters later: score **zero**. (Saga, not survey — treat it as legend.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Mosfellsdalur

en: **The dig:** archaeologists have excavated nearby at **Hrísbrú**, where the saga says Egil's bones were later moved to the church his descendants built.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Mosfellsdalur

en: **The Nobel:** born **Halldór Guðjónsson** in **1902**, raised from age three at the farm **Laxnes** just here in the valley — when he needed an author's name, **he took the farm's**. **Nobel Prize for Literature, 1955**, largely for ***Sjálfstætt fólk*** (*Independent People*).

en: That farm on the left started with **six horses and one stranger asking for a ride.** Its horses have since turned up in *Game of Thrones* — and the boy who grew up on this land carried the farm's name all the way to Stockholm.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm

en: **Ragnheiður Gíslason** and **Þórarinn "Þóri" Jónasson** moved onto the run-down farm in **1967** and started the riding business in **1968**, after a visitor asked out of nowhere whether they'd take him out on horseback. Six horses, summers only. It grew into **Iceland's oldest continuously running riding-tour company** — **120 horses** and around **15,000 riders a year** by **2018**, **85% of them from abroad**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm

en: Their horses work on screen too. The Mosfellsbær local paper *Mosfellingur* puts it plainly: **"hestar frá Laxnesi birst í nokkrum bíómyndum eins og Game of Thrones"** — horses from Laxnes have appeared in several films, *Game of Thrones* among them. In **1992** Þóri shipped Icelandic horses to the **United States** to show them off near Hollywood and ended up on **CBS and CNN**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm

en: And the name. **Halldór Guðjónsson** was raised on this farm from the age of **three**. When he started publishing he took the farm's name — **Laxness** — and in **1955** that name won Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature**. The house he built, **Gljúfrasteinn**, is **600 metres further up the valley**: our next stop.

en: The Poet's House

en: On **17 June 1945** — the young republic's first birthday — a woman sat down and typed the building contract for that white house. **Ten years later there was a Nobel Prize in it.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: The typist was **Auður Sveinsdóttir**, born at **Eyrarbakki on 30 July 1918**, and she didn't just type it — she ran the build. She married **Halldór Laxness** that **Christmas Eve, 1945**. The architect was **Ágúst Pálsson**; the house was home from **1945** until Halldór died on **8 February 1998**. Auður outlived him by fourteen years, dying **29 October 2012**, aged **94**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **1955:** Halldór takes Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — *"for his vivid epic power which has renewed the great narrative art of Iceland."* Auður marked it the way a textile artist would: she made **Maríuklæðið**, "Mary's Cloth", to commemorate it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **Kjarval's altarpieces, chapter one:** in **1914** he painted one for **Bakkagerði** church out east — Christ preaching from **Álfaborg**, the elf-rock, **Dyrfjöll** behind. The bishop refused to bless it — **too many elves, not enough Jesus**. It still hangs there, gloriously **unconsecrated**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: **Chapter two:** his second altarpiece (*John the Baptist, Christ at his feet*) was rejected outright as **"crude and ugly"** — so **Halldór bought the reject and gave it a wall in this house.** One man, two altarpieces, **zero bishops convinced** — and the painter, the brewer's Viking and the novelist, the morning's three pocket names, all tie off in this one valley.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en: The **Icelandic state bought the house and its art in 2002**, a hundred years to the year since Halldór was born, and opened it to the public on **4 September 2004**. His **typewriter is still on the desk**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn

en:
🔥 793  Lindisfarne raid — traditional start of the Viking Age
   825  Faroe Islands settlement begins
   841  Dublin founded as a Viking longphort
🔑 862  Rurik arrives in Novgorod
🔥 870  Iceland settlement begins (Ingólfr Arnarson)
🔥 878  Peace of Wedmore (Danelaw boundary set by the later Alfred–Guthrum treaty)
   882  Oleg takes Kiev — founds Kievan Rus'
🔑 911  Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte creates Normandy
🔥 930  Alþingi established in Iceland
🔥 985  Erik the Red settles Greenland
🔥 1000 Leif Erikson reaches Vínland (N. America)
🔑 1066 Battle of Stamford Bridge — end of the Viking Age

en: By tradition, in **874 CE** Iceland was all but empty. By **930**, it was full. Settled, mapped and **booted up with a national parliament** — in a single human lifetime.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The **Landnám** ("Land-Taking") is the **~60-year window** when 9,000-plus Norse, Celtic and other settlers grabbed every habitable bay and valley on the island. (**874 is the traditional date**; Ari the Wise points nearer **870**, and a nationwide ash layer — the **871 ± 2 tephra** — timestamps the whole business to the second.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The textbook source is **Landnámabók** (*The Book of Settlements*) — **400 settlers** named, their farms, feuds and home-towns mapped in detail no other Viking-age country can match.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: The trick: Iceland had **no locals to fight** — just a handful of Irish monks (the **Papar**) who legged it the moment longships appeared.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏘️ Landnám

en: By **930** the population (and the feuds) were big enough that the chieftains met at **Þingvellir** to launch the **Alþingi**, the world's oldest parliament still in use.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: You are in the **gap between two continents** — and no, they do not meet here. They are tearing **apart**, at the speed your fingernails grow, and this valley is the hole they have left behind.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you are standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here. The valley **is** the gap.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: The cracks have names. **Almannagjá**, the big one you are walking through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it is the seam, still ripping.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: It does not creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the assembly ground.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m.** The parliament you are about to stand in met noticeably higher up than the ground you are on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Almannagjá

en: 🎬 **On screen:** this gorge is the pass to the **Bloody Gate** in *Game of Thrones* — the gate was added digitally above the Öxarárfoss trail — and the park doubled as an otherworldly realm in ***Thor: The Dark World*** (2013).

en: ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: At the Law Rock — the wall behind you is the reason this spot was chosen.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: No royal palace. No marble columns. Just a rock, a cliff wall, and the world's first national parliament held outdoors.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: Britain calls itself the home of parliament. Iceland was running one **300 years before the Magna Carta** — in a hole in the ground.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: Iceland's First Parliament
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: The **world's oldest parliament still in use**. Set up in **930 CE** in a literal **crack in the earth** — because the acoustics were better than anyone's farmhouse.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: In **930 CE**, Iceland's chieftains gathered here and founded the **Alþingi** — the national assembly. They picked the spot because the **Lögberg** ("Law Rock") cliff wall **carried the spoken law** across the valley.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: For two weeks every summer the country **shut down** and came here: laws made, marriages arranged, murderers tried, beer drunk.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: The **Lögsögumaður** (Law-Speaker), elected for a **three-year term**, had to recite **a third of the entire legal code from memory each year** — three years to deliver the lot. Drop one clause and you could change a verdict.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: And there was **no king** — roughly **36 goðar** (chieftain-priests) ran the whole thing by consensus. One law, one people, zero crowns.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: They chose this ground carefully: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: It met here every summer until **1798**, sat two more summers in Reykjavík, and was then **abolished outright by royal decree on 6 June 1800.** Re-established on **8 March 1843**, it sat again on **1 July 1845** — in Reykjavík, in a school building. So not a thousand unbroken years. A thousand years with a **43-year hole** that Denmark put there.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: the national assembly founded here in 930
ctx: gloss for the name "Alþingi" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: the Law Rock, the cliff wall that carried the spoken law across the valley
ctx: gloss for the name "Lögberg" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi

en: ⚖️ Kristnitaka
ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Standing at Lögberg. This is the exact ground where it was decided.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Most national religions are imposed by kings or won by armies. Iceland's was decided **on this rock, by a man having a lie-down.**
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Calmly, collectively, and after a really good night's sleep. That is how Iceland became Christian — standing where you are standing. Most countries were not given the option.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: The Day Iceland Changed Religion, Lying Down
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Around **the year 1000**, Iceland changed its national religion **without a single sword being drawn** — right here. No army. No martyrs. Just one pagan chieftain, one cloak, and a really long nap.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: By **999** the country was split — Christian districts against pagan strongholds — and Norway's King **Ólafur Tryggvason** was squeezing hard: he welcomed Christian traders into his ports, barred the pagans, and **held Icelandic hostages** as leverage. Convert, or lose the trade route you cannot live without.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Persuasion had gone badly. One Saxon priest, **Þangbrandur**, allegedly **fought duels and killed poets** who mocked his sermons. Not a charm offensive.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: By **AD 1000** (the sources wobble between 999 and 1000) the **Alþingi** met on this spot facing two religions, two law codes and one looming civil war — so both sides handed the verdict to one man: **Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði**, the *pagan* Law-Speaker.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: He lay down under his cloak **a full day and a night**, then stood up on this rock and ruled: **one law, one people, one faith — Christianity** — so the young commonwealth would not split in two. Private sacrifice, horse-meat and infant exposure were quietly tolerated at first, then dropped. Food is food.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: the pagan Law-Speaker who lay under his cloak a day and a night, then chose Christianity
ctx: gloss for the name "Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: the Saxon priest who fought duels with the poets who mocked his sermons
ctx: gloss for the name "Þangbrandur" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: Norway's king, who squeezed Iceland with port bans and hostages
ctx: gloss for the name "Ólafur Tryggvason" — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kristnitaka

en: ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The white church and the five-gabled farmhouse on your right, at the bottom of the wall.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: A thousand-year-old church, a Prime Minister's summer house, and a national shrine containing two poets — one of whom may not be the right man.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: They built this to hold the greatest Icelanders who ever lived. Two people went in. Then everyone thought about it a bit more and decided, actually, we'd rather be buried at home.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: A Westminster Abbey With Two Occupants
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: There has been a church on this spot since **1017**. Beside it is a **national burial ground built to hold Iceland's greatest artists** — and in eighty-five years it has managed to bury exactly **two people**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The church first went up around **1017**, the present building dates from **1859**, and the bell tower was added in **1907** — the date is on the weather vane. It has no resident priest; the one who serves it **comes out from Skálholt**, which we pass later today.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The five-gabled farmhouse beside it is **Þingvallabær**, built in **1930** for the Alþingi millennium festival by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, the state architect. He turned its face deliberately toward **Almannagjá** — the older turf farmhouse it replaced had looked out at the lake. It began with **three gables**; two more were added after a **1970 fire** destroyed the king's house next door. Since **1974** it has been the **Prime Minister's summer residence.** One gable belongs to the church.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Behind the church is **Skáldareitur**, the poets' plot — and it exists because of an argument over a corpse. When **Einar Benediktsson** died in **January 1940**, his ex-wife and his companion could not agree who had the right to bury him. **Jónas Jónsson frá Hriflu** saw the opening and proposed a national honour ground here, modelled on **Westminster Abbey**. Einar went into it on **27 January 1940**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: The second and last arrival was **Jónas Hallgrímsson**, Iceland's national poet, who had died in Copenhagen on **26 May 1845** of blood poisoning after breaking his leg on a staircase. His bones came home and were buried here on **16 November 1946** — over the objection of the man who dug them up, who wanted him in **Öxnadalur** where he was born. The Prime Minister, **Ólafur Thors**, overruled him. The government's position was that **Jónas's bones were state property.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: And nobody is sure they are his. Two other people had been buried on top of him in **1875** and **1900**, and both had to be lifted out first. The doubt has never gone away — there are still calls to open the grave and test what is in it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Two graves. That is the whole national pantheon. **Halldór Laxness**, whose house we passed this morning, is not here. **Kjarval**, who opened this tour, is not here either. Iceland built itself a Westminster Abbey and then quietly stopped using it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur

en: Follow the Öxará. The waterfall ahead, the still green pool below it, and the coin-filled crack by the bridge.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The law was spoken up on the rock. It was carried out down here, in the water.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: People throw coins in and make a wish because a sign in the 1930s told them to. Icelanders have been quietly watching tourists do it ever since and saying nothing.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The Waterfall, the Drowning Pool and the Fake Wishing Well
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: A waterfall that was **moved here on purpose**, a pool where **at least eighteen women were drowned**, and a wishing well invented by **a sign put up in the 1930s.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The **Öxará** comes over the wall at **Öxarárfoss** and runs down through the assembly ground. It is the main open river feeding the whole valley — and it is doing a job it was very probably given, diverted to bring water to the assembly.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: Below the falls the river widens into a still green pool: **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**; women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** were **drowned here**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749.** A memorial plaque now names them. Two weeks a year this place made the law. It also carried out the sentence.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: And then there is **Peningagjá** — the crack full of coins by the bridge, properly the southern end of **Nikulásargjá**. The coins have nothing to do with the sagas. The **bridge went up in 1907** for the visit of the Danish king **Frederick VIII**, who is said to have thrown the first one in.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: The wish came later, and from a signpost. In the **1930s** somebody put up a board reading **"to the wishing well"** — and that is the entire origin of the tradition. The national park's own record is blunt about it: **no older Icelandic folk tale or story about wishing here exists.** An ancient custom, ninety years old, invented by signage.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá

en: 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
ctx: block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The lake filling the rift ahead of you, and the clear pools off to the side.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Two continents pulling apart, the cleanest drinking water on the planet running through the gap, and a fish quietly turning into four other fish while nobody watches.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Iceland's answer to a tectonic disaster: turn it into a reservoir, then drink it.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The Cleanest Water on Earth, and Four Fish That Are One Fish
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: Meltwater that left a glacier **thirty to a hundred years ago**, filtered through lava the whole way — **drinkable from your cupped hand**, with **120 m** of underwater visibility. And one fish in it that has quietly become four.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: **Þingvallavatn** is Iceland's largest natural lake: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, averaging **34 m**, sitting at roughly **100.5 m above sea level** — and its bed lies **below sea level** because of the rifting.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: About **nine-tenths of everything entering it arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava at **3–4°C**. Only about a tenth comes in as visible surface water, most of that the **Öxará**. The catchment runs to some **1,300 km²**, of which the lake is only about **six per cent** — the rest is plumbing you cannot see.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces. Clear pools like **Silfra** are that meltwater arriving. The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years.** **Kuðungableikja**, the snail charr. **Dvergbleikja**, the dwarf. **Murta**, the small open-water one. **Sílableikja**, the fish-eater. Two feed on the bottom, two feed in open water — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: **Three of the four are genetically distinct.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out muddled — some read as murta, others as crosses. Vísindavefurinn's assessment is that this may be **sympatric speciation**, one population dividing with no physical barrier between the halves, and that another **10,000 years** could produce genuinely separate species. Evolution has not finished tidying up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: That island out in the lake is **Sandey**, a **tuff cone** built by **Hengill** about **1,900 years ago** — the same eruption that laid down **Nesjahraun** at the north end. An eruption happened in the middle of a lake and built itself an island out of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra

en: The Republic, in the Rain
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944

en: On **17 June 1944** Iceland declared itself a republic — not in the capital, but **here**, in the rain, in front of tens of thousands of people standing in this valley.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944

en: They could have done it in Reykjavík, in a building, dry. They chose this ground instead: **the place the nation first assembled in 930**, and the place Denmark had shut down in **1800**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944

en: The date was not an accident either — **17 June** is the birthday of **Jón Sigurðsson**, the man who led the independence campaign and who did not live to see it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944

en: It rained. It rained hard, the whole way through. Nobody left. The photographs of that day are mostly a valley full of soaked people refusing to go home.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🇮🇸 17 June 1944

en: On a very, very clear day this same sightline stacks up **three more ice-capped volcanoes** toward the coast: **Tindfjallajökull**, then **Eyjafjallajökull** — of 2010 ash-cloud fame — then **Mýrdalsjökull** behind it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: She is a great deal older than her CV suggests. The story of the Hekla we would recognise today begins **just over 7,000 years ago** — she was already in business long before anyone was here to take notes. **1104** was her **first eruption after the settlement of Iceland** — and it is still **her own largest explosive eruption in historical time.** (The bigger explosive eruption in Iceland's historical record belongs to a rival: **Öræfajökull in 1362.**) She had been quiet for roughly **three centuries** beforehand, which means nobody then alive had the faintest idea what she was capable of.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: The ash of 1104 went north, and the farming districts of **Þjórsárdalur** and **Hrunamannahreppur** were **abandoned** because of it. Iceland got a thousand years of European publicity out of that eruption and **wrote none of it** — the people actually living underneath were otherwise engaged, emptying two districts.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: The Judas story has a date and a document. **Within ten to twenty years of 1104** an **English poem** was already asserting that **Judas** — the arch-traitor himself — was imprisoned inside Hekla, and European clergy positively welcomed eruption reports, because to their minds an eruption **proved that Hell existed.** The image that fixed it was a woodcut in the history of the Northern Peoples by the Swedish churchman **Olaus Magnus (1490–1557)**, published in **Venice in 1555**, showing Hekla with a set of tunnels running down out of the mountain. **Vesuvius and Etna never acquired the same reputation** — and Vísindavefur offers the driest explanation available. They were **too close to civilisation.** A volcano safely off the edge of Europe made a far more convincing front door.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🌋 Hekla

en: Her longest eruption began on **5 April 1766** and continued with breaks until **May 1768** — **just over two years**, including a **six-month pause** in the middle that must have felt to everyone like the end of it.

en: **Brúará** ("Bridge-River") is a clear, spring-fed river feeding the Hvítá; its showpiece is the electric-blue waterfall **Brúarfoss**. For centuries a natural **stone arch** here was the only crossing for miles.

Charity, Skálholt-style: demolish the bridge so the hungry can't walk over it.

en: Iceland ran itself as a republic for **300 years**. Then **one family** decided that wasn't working — and burned the whole thing down. Literally.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: The **Sturlungaöld** ran roughly **1220–1262** — Iceland's longest, ugliest internal war.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Power had pooled in a few big clans, especially the **Sturlungar** (yes, saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**'s family). Disputes stopped going to the Althing and started going to **swords, fires and assassinations**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: **Spring 1238, at Apavatn** — the lake we just passed — **Sturla Sighvatsson** ambushed his rival **Gizur Þorvaldsson** of the Haukdælir and forced him to **swear on the Bible** to give up power and sail to Norway. Gizur had his fingers crossed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Five months later the oath came due at **Örlygsstaðir (21 August 1238)** — Gizur, teamed up with **Kolbeinn ungi**, brought **~1,700 men against ~1,000** to the **largest battle ever fought on Icelandic soil**. The northern Sturlungar were wiped out in an afternoon; Sturla's ancient family spear **Grásíða kept bending in his hands** as the tide turned, and Gizur is said to have struck the fatal blow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Snorri himself — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was **murdered in his own cellar at Reykholt on 23 September 1241**, on the orders of the Norwegian king, by a raiding party led by **Gizur Þorvaldsson, his own former son-in-law**. His last words: ***"Eigi skal höggva!"*** — "Don't strike!" They struck.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: The low point: the **Burning of Flugumýri (1253)** — a wedding ambush, the hall torched with the family inside. (Often linked to *Game of Thrones'* Red Wedding — a pop claim; see verify list.)

en: **Haukadalur** means **"Valley of the Hawks"** — known now for steam, but for two centuries this was a **chieftain's seat**: the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth.

en: **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — settled this farm and became the **patriarch of the Haukdælir**. He ran a famous school here in the 11th century, and one of its boarders, from about **age seven**, was **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148) — who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, the reason Iceland has any firm early dates at all. (The *first*-school crown belongs to **Skálholt**, down the road — we'll get there.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: The family stayed at the top for two centuries — bishops, lawmen, and finally **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, the oath-breaker of Örlygsstaðir from the last stop: a **Haukdæling**, made **Iceland's first and only earl in 1258**, four years before the republic he helped bury was handed to Norway.

en: The field sits on the **Hreppar block** — water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam, shoots back up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, most recently **June 2000** — then dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The world's most famous Icelandic conservation story — lost in the courtroom, saved in the end, by a woman who never had a vote.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: An investor showed up with engineers. A farmer's daughter showed up and lost every legal round — and the falls are still here.

en: Meltwater and the Falls One Woman Saved
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: In **1907** an investor tried to dam this waterfall — and a farmer's daughter, **Sigríður**, fought it all the way to Reykjavík. She **lost in court** — and the falls are still here anyway.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: **Gullfoss** ("Golden Falls") drops the **Hvítá** down two staircase tiers, **32 m** total, in a narrow canyon — spray throwing rainbows so consistently it looks staged.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The Hvítá is **glacial meltwater** from **Langjökull**, silt-laden enough to glow gold in summer light.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: **Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: Forty-three tracks in three acts, and the whole story of how a country with fewer people than most cities ended up on everybody's playlist. We get through the first two today.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT I — Borrowed clothes.** Iceland still working out who it sounds like. Five of the biggest singalongs here are secretly Anglo-American hits in Icelandic disguise — *Mambo Italiano*, *California Dreamin'*, *I Will*, Ray Sharpe rockabilly, and a Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm. The mambo arrived secondhand, via 1950s Manhattan. Post-war crooners, dancehall ballads, and Keflavík kids who saw The Beatles in Bournemouth and ran home to start a band.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **01 · Jeg vil ha' morfor med mig ud på sjov** — *Raquel Rastenni*. Plot twist — the Danes nicked it. The song is actually “Jag ska' ta' morfar med mej ut i kväll,” a 1949 Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm, dressed up in a Danish coat a year later. Same writers (Peter Spar / Jessup Sandy), different *morfar*.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **02 · Litla flugan** — *Sigfús Halldórsson*. Iceland's most beloved earworm started as a bar bet. December 1951, Reykhólar farm — the manager Sigurður Elíasson tells Sigfús he can't turn that poem into a tune in ten minutes. Ten minutes later: a national standard. Drinks were *not* on Sigurður.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **03 · Bláu augun** — *Haukur Morthens*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **04 · Vor við flóann** — *Ragnar Bjarnason*. Two-for-one. The 1959 7″ gives you Ragnar singing “Vor við flóann” on the A-side — flip it over and **Guðbergur Auðunsson** takes the mic for “Hvítir svanir.” Same record, two singers, no warning.  [Recorded somewhere unusual]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **05 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **06 · Hæ Mambó** — *Haukur Morthens*. Yes — *that* Mambo Italiano. The Rosemary Clooney one. Loftur Guðmundsson Icelanded the lyrics and Reykjavík caught the mambo bug secondhand via 1950s Manhattan.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **07 · Lilla Jóns** — *Guðbergur Auðunsson*. It's a Ray Sharpe rockabilly tune in Icelandic drag. Jón Sigurðsson took the American melody, dressed it in his own words, and out came “Little Jónsi.”  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **08 · Sveitapiltsins draumur** — *Hljómar*. California Dreamin'. With Icelandic lyrics. About a country boy. Yes, really.  [Secret-cover thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **09 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **10 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **11 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT II — Finding the voice.** Iceland stops borrowing and starts getting copied. *Með allt á hreinu* eats half the country's box office — **120,000 tickets, 230,000 people**. Grýlurnar weaponise punk, and the band rivalry becomes the actual plot of the film. The Sugarcubes go global. Björk goes solo. GusGus turn out to be a twelve-person filmmaking collective who picked up instruments halfway through.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **17 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **18 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **19 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **20 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **21 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **22 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **23 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **24 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **25 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **26 · Serenade** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Album closer of *Fisherman's Woman* (Rough Trade, 2005). Torrini said the entire album was “a letter I wrote to a person that I lost at that time. I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: We grow **tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and strawberries** at the latitude of **Fairbanks, Alaska** — heated by hot water that **costs us almost nothing**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its star farm — a working geothermal greenhouse complex where you can eat lunch among the vines.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Inside, roughly **ten thousand tomato plants** grow under LED lights on **geothermal water** piped straight from the ground, pollinated by **imported Dutch bumblebees** — Iceland has no native pollinator strong enough for tomato flowers, so it flew in a workforce.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The signature dish is **unlimited tomato soup eaten three feet from the plants that made it**. Same volcanic heat that warms Reykjavík's homes, just aimed at lunch.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse went up in 1924**, over in **Mosfellssveit**, once growers worked out that geothermal water could both **heat the glasshouse and steam-sterilise the soil**. Here at Reykholt the first greenhouse went up at **Reykholtshver in 1932**, and the **first proper horticultural station followed in 1938**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: **Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** took Friðheimar over in **1995**, built the first large house between **1995 and 2001**, and switched to **year-round tomatoes in 2002**. Before that, Icelandic tomatoes simply stopped in winter.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal energy gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **electric grow-lights** through the dark months. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The horse in that field is a **direct descendant of a Viking horse** — a bloodline effectively **closed for ~1,000 years**. Just don't call it a pony. That's the one hill Iceland will genuinely die on.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: The **Icelandic horse** is small (**~132–145 cm**), shaggy, long-lived (often **30 years**), tough and frankly opinionated — and by breed convention and national insistence, **always a "horse," never a pony**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: No new bloodstock has arrived since roughly the year **1000**, so it's essentially a **closed, disease-naïve population** — one of the purest native breeds on Earth. Tradition says the **Alþingi** slammed the import door around **982**; the documented ban dates to **1882** — and it still stands.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: Most breeds have three or four gaits; the Icelandic has up to **five**, including the famous **tölt** — a four-beat running walk so smooth you could carry a full beer and not spill it. The extra gaits trace to a **single gene mutation**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: Population ~**78,000** in Iceland and ~**195,000 abroad** across 30+ countries — the diaspora outnumbers the home herd two to one, and **not one of them is ever allowed back** (biosecurity enforced by MAST, the food and veterinary authority).

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: For **700 years**, this farm was Iceland's **capital, university and cathedral** rolled into one. Then a **1784 earthquake** ate the lot — and the country never gave it back.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: **Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** (Skálholtsskóli, 1056), a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: It gave Iceland its **only saint** — **Þorlákur Þórhallsson**, declared holy by the Alþingi in **1198** and formally made **patron saint of Iceland by the Vatican in 1984**; his feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The **Reformation** arrived on **7 November 1550** with the beheading here of **Jón Arason** — the Catholic bishop of *Hólar*, the northern see — and two of his sons. The Lutheran takeover, sealed in blood on this lawn.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: A **~magnitude-7 earthquake** (South Iceland Seismic Zone) in **1784** levelled the cathedral; the Danes used it to abolish the bishopric and shift the see to a fishing village called **Reykjavík** — formally, in **1801**. (The last bishop to live at Skálholt, **Hannes Finnsson**, died here in **1796**; the lights went out slowly.) The current church is a **1963 reconstruction** — where the blues-rock band **Kaleo** later recorded a track live, because Iceland.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: Its first bishop, from **1056**, was **Ísleifur Gissurarson** — whose son ran the school up at **Haukadalur**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The district around it is **Biskupstungur**, **the bishop's tongues** — the wedge of land between the **Hvítá** and the **Tungufljót**. A **tunga** is a tongue of land between two rivers, and the bishop in the name is the one on that hill.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The church came before the bishop. **Gissur hvíti** — Ísleifur's own father — is said to have raised the **first church at Skálholt** after the conversion at the **Alþingi in the year 1000**, and **Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated the first bishop of Iceland in 1056** and took his seat there. Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The school ran from **the later eleventh century until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The 1550 beheading has names and a run-up. **Jón Arason** was executed here on **7 November 1550** together with his sons **Ari** and **the Reverend Björn** — and two years earlier, in **1548**, the Skálholt men had thrown up a **fort east of the churchyard** to hold off his attack, the remains of which are still identifiable on the ground. In **1912** an Englishwoman, **Disney Leith**, paid for a **monument** to him at what is taken to be the execution spot.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The site carries **ten protected archaeological monuments** and **well over a hundred** further age-protected remains. The cathedral standing there now was designed by the state architect **Hörður Bjarnason** and consecrated in **1963** — and Skálholt got a bishop back, a **vígslubiskup**, in **1992.** (Seven hundred years as the centre of the country, ended by an earthquake rather than by politics.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛪ Skálholt

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **Kerið** is a **5,000–6,000-year-old volcanic crater** — about **270 m long, 170 m wide and 55 m deep**: enough to swallow a **17-storey building**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: The walls are **red scoria** — iron-rich basalt cinders whose iron has **oxidised to hematite**, rust essentially, helped along by groundwater; give it a few thousand more years and it'll blacken like its neighbours. The lake is **groundwater** (7–14 m deep) with **no inlet or outlet** — it just tracks the water table, turquoise because the water absorbs red light first against a dark floor. There's even life in it: a **2014 study found 10 kinds of zooplankton**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: **Kerið** is a **gjallgígur** — a scoria crater, built up from cinder. It is **not** an explosion crater. The eruption that made it took its time about it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: Kerið is **privately owned** — by **Kerfélagið**, an association of the local landowners — and has charged a small **admission fee since 2013**, which is unusual in a country where walking into a landscape is normally free. The money goes on the path and the **stairway down the north wall**, which is how you get to stand at the water's edge.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: It sits in the **Grímsnes** volcanic field on the western rift — the northernmost of a four-crater row, and the work of **one of a dozen or so Grímsnes eruptions** that built the **Grímsneshraun** lava field. (No single big bang, then — this one was built up slowly, the way Iceland does most things.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

en: The bowl's acoustics are superb, so it's hosted **concerts on a floating stage**. The famous first, in **August 1987**, drew ~**5,000 people** and was headlined by the operatic bass **Kristinn Sigmundsson**; a 21-year-old **Björk** (then in the early Sugarcubes) was on the bill too — real, but not the headliner the postcards promise.

en: The **Sog** flows out of **Þingvallavatn** (Iceland's biggest natural lake) and joins the Hvítá to form the Ölfusá.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Short but huge in volume — **Iceland's largest clearwater (spring-fed) river**, ~**110 m³/s** of glacier-filtered, lake-clear water, perfect for hydro.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Three plants — **Ljósafoss**, **Írafoss** and **Steingrímsstöð**, built **1937–1959** — a combined **~90 MW** that together ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s and 70s, until the bigger highland plants on the **Þjórsá** took over.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: And where did Iceland's electric age actually start? Not here — in a **carpenter's workshop in Hafnarfjörður**: on **12 December 1904**, **Jóhannes Reykdal** switched on the country's **first power station**, lighting **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus his own workshop and four street lamps**, in time for Christmas. From one carpenter's stream to all of this, in a single lifetime.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: The consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited. **Steingrímsstöð** very nearly did not happen either — its dam **gave way during construction in the storm of 17 June 1959.** Losing a dam on the national day is not a detail Icelanders bring up often.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: Also one of Iceland's best **brown trout** rivers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: **Ljósafossstöð** was built between **1935 and 1937**, and opened with **two machines totalling 8.8 MW** (two of **4.4 MW**). A **third machine of 5.8 MW** was added in **1944**, taking it to its **14.6 MW** installed — about **105 GWh** a year. Scale was never the point. **Being first was.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: The reason the engineers loved this river: the **Sog is the only river draining Þingvallavatn**, and that lake behaves like an enormous header tank — it refuses to flood and it refuses to dry. That makes the Sog **one of the steadiest rivers in the country**, which is exactly what a turbine wants.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River

en: A town of **about 3,350 people** where the ground occasionally rearranges itself — and the locals responded by **building an exhibition around the crack in their floor**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Hveragerði sits on a **three-way tectonic junction** on the edge of the **Hengill volcanic system** — so geothermal that fumaroles and mud pots vent **between the houses**. On **29 May 2008** the ground let go twice inside three seconds — a **doublet**: **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault about 5 km to the west**, a **composite Mw 6.1** that split buildings and re-plumbed the town's hot springs.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Rather than hide it, locals built the **Skjálftinn 2008** ("The Quake") exhibition inside the **Sunnumörk** shopping centre — right over a fissure the quake tore through the building. Stand on the crack, ride the shaking simulator.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Cheap volcanic heat made it a **greenhouse town** from the 1920s (Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse** went up in **1924**, over in **Mosfellssveit**): tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers — and, at the horticultural college, **experimental bananas** (about a tonne a year, purely a science project — Iceland is *not* a banana republic).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: The town has a birthday. It began in **1929**, on land belonging to the farm **Vorsabær** in Ölfus: that summer the milk station went up at **Breiðumörk 26**, and the first two houses appeared — **Varmahlíð**, and a summer house at **Fagrihvammur** where **ylrækt**, growing under glass on geothermal heat, started in Hveragerði. A milk station, two dwellings and a greenhouse. That is the whole origin.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them went straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective could: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flower growing took off across the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today, 3,344 at the start of 2026.** The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged the 2008 quake to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, announced that afternoon at magnitude **6.3** (the Met Office's English release settles on **6.1** for the composite event), epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. And the best thing in **Sunnumörk** was never meant to be an exhibit at all: when the centre was under construction in **2003** an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at **over 6 on the Richter scale.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
