en: Sixteen tracks, sequenced for exactly this road: quiet while you are tired, warm as the light changes, loud by the time the city shows up.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT I — Silence.** You have been awake since six and the whole day is in your bones. Piano, strings, glass-cool modern classical, and a lullaby to close it. That lullaby, track three, is — heads up — technically about infanticide. We will not dwell.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **01 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **02 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **03 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT II — Eyes Open.** The warmth creeps in. Laufey waltzes. **Elín Hall** sings about her dad running *toward* the lava — not a metaphor, in a country built on the stuff. **Ásgeir's** actual father writes his son a song called *The Journey Home*, and the bus suddenly knows where it is going. Then BRÍET, Friðrik Dór and Jón Jónsson, and Valdimar lift it up off the floor.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **04 · Bewitched** — *Laufey*. Title track of the 2023 album that won Laufey the Grammy for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album in 2024. She wrote it as a “guitar voice waltz” about the moment of falling helplessly into new love after a perfect first date — then asked the **Philharmonia Orchestra** to score the inside of her head. She calls it the song that “sets the sound of the album.” One song. One orchestra. One Grammy. Done.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **05 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **06 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **07 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **08 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **09 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **ACT III — Bags Packed.** Reykjavík widens ahead and the volume comes up. Of Monsters and Men, then **Una Stef** singing *Like Home* — her father wrote track 39 of the other playlist. Agent Fresco blow the doors off. Reykjavík's own mystery woman finally gets a name, seventy years late. Quarashi, and then **Ingó Veðurguð** has the last word.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **10 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **11 · Like Home** — *Una Stef*. Keep track 39 of the other playlist in mind. *Á Góðum Degi* is by **Stefán S. Stefánsson** — and Una Stef is his daughter. Two playlists, one family, and a song called *Like Home* arriving right as Reykjavík comes back into view. Neither of us planned that.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Friðrik Dór*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke. Friðrik Dór cut this reworking in **2016**; his melody line wanders a fair way from Jón Múli’s original.  [Family wrote it]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: In most countries, a volcano is a disaster plan. In Iceland, it's the **light switch**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system**, a rare **plate-boundary triple junction on dry land**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines — the white plumes are **steam**, not smoke. Built up in stages 2006–2011 to **303 MW**, it's **Iceland's largest geothermal power station**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: After the electricity, the leftover hot water pipes off to heat **more than half of the capital region** — nothing wasted.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' Mammoth** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: The trick that makes the whole thing work: the geothermal fluid under us is **hot, corrosive and loaded with dissolved minerals**, and it never goes anywhere near your radiator. It is used to **heat clean groundwater through heat exchangers**, and that clean heated water is what travels to the city. **You get the heat without the chemistry.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Hellisheiði's quieter half is the hot water: **200 MW of thermal output**, about **950 litres per second** down the pipe. Over the ridge sits its older sibling **Nesjavellir** — **Reykjavík bought the farm in 1965** and production still did not begin until **1990**, which is **twenty-five years** of drilling, testing and arguing before one useful litre went anywhere. It now runs at **up to 120 MW of electricity** and **up to 300 MW of thermal**, or as Orka náttúrunnar puts it in the only unit a household understands: **1,640 litres of hot water every second.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Nesjavellir has grown hard. In the late **1990s** the same station was being reported to Alþingi at **60 MW of electricity and 200 MW of heat** — **the electrical output has since doubled and the heat output is up by half**, on the same hillside, with the same rock. Between the two stations, **Orka náttúrunnar supplies roughly 60 per cent of all the hot water in the capital region.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: **Hengill** is not a peak, it is a **volcanic system 50 to 60 kilometres long** and **5 to 10 kilometres wide**, running from **Selvogur** in the south-west all the way up to **Þingvallavatn**. Its most recent eruptions, about **1,900 years ago**, produced **Nesjahraun** and part of **Hellisheiðarhraun**; an earlier round **5,700 to 5,800 years ago** produced **Hagavíkurhraun**. It is **classified as active** — and this power station was built on that basis, not in spite of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Nationally, **about 90 per cent of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes comes from geothermal** — that is Orkustofnun's figure for **2020.** The comparable British number is effectively **zero.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **~5,000 years ago** lava from the **Leiti** shield volcano rolled over the **Heiðmörk** wetland; trapped water flashed to steam and, in a **phreatomagmatic** blast, **punched back out** through the molten lava — frozen mid-explosion in red scoria (iron oxide — rust).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: Originally ~**80 cones**. Because a rootless cone only forms where lava met water, geologists read Iceland's as a template for **Mars** — the rootless cones of **Athabasca Valles** are cited as evidence of buried water on the Red Planet.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: Then, practically, the British army mined the field for gravel to build **Reykjavík airport** in WWII; digging continued for years. Protected in **1974**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: One full-circle glance before the city: behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn** — and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**, the only ground anyone has ever dug an assembly out of from this era: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring**, protected since **1930** as *the ancient Kjalarnesþing site*. Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, nobody has ever proven — so you're leaving the Golden Circle past the country's first parliament grounds. Probably.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: And the electricity story closes here too: the **Elliðaár** valley below held **Reykjavík's first power station (1921)** — seventeen years after **Reykdal's carpentry-shop plant** lit the nation's first bulbs in Hafnarfjörður. From a workshop stream to a volcano filing CO₂ as gravel: one century of Icelandic power, and you've just driven the whole arc.

en: **Haukadalur** means **"Valley of the Hawks"** — known now for steam, but historically one of Iceland's great **education centres**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: In the 11th century the farm was home to **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — who ran a **famous school** at the farm (the *first*-school crown belongs to **Skálholt**). One of its boarders, from about **age seven**: **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148), who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, Iceland's foundational history and the reason we have any firm early dates at all.

en: That waterfall you just photographed at Gullfoss? It's **this glacier crying.** Now we're going to ride snowmobiles across the thing doing the crying — a **580-metre-thick bank of ice, currently in overdraft.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **Langjökull** means **"Long Glacier"** — Icelandic place-naming at its most ruthlessly literal, like nicknaming a tall bloke "Tall Man." It's **Iceland's second-largest ice cap** (after Vatnajökull): roughly **870–900 km²**, about **50 km long, up to 20 km wide**, holding on the order of **190 km³ of ice** up to **~580 m thick** and topping out just over **1,400 metres**. You'll be snowmobiling on more frozen water than most countries own.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **Fire directly under the ice:** this isn't just frozen scenery — it's a **lid on two active volcanic systems**, **Prestahnúkur** and **Hveravellir**. The calm white surface you're carving across has a temper it simply hasn't used lately.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **The waterworks of the whole Golden Circle:** Langjökull's meltwater feeds the **Hvítá** — the river that becomes **Gullfoss** — plus the **Ölfusá** system, and, via groundwater filtered through porous lava, the eerily clear **Silfra** fissure back at Þingvellir. Everything wet you've seen today drained off the glacier under your skis.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: **The timer:** Langjökull has been **losing mass steadily for decades**, and Institute of Earth Sciences modelling projects it could be **largely gone within about 150 years** on present warming — the fastest-shrinking of Iceland's big caps. Snowmobiling here is less "extreme sport," more "**visiting a patient you'll outlive.**"
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: For the fully indoors version, the **"Into the Glacier"** ice tunnel — the world's largest man-made bore into a glacier, **~500 m** long, opened **1 June 2015** from the Húsafell side — lets you walk *inside* Langjökull past ice older than the settlement of Iceland. A museum you have to dig.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull

en: The walls are **red scoria** — iron-rich basalt cinders whose iron has **oxidised to hematite**, rust essentially, helped along by groundwater; give it a few thousand more years and it'll blacken like its neighbours. The lake is **groundwater** (7–14 m deep) with **no inlet or outlet** — it just tracks the water table, turquoise because the water absorbs red light first against a dark floor. There's even life in it: a 2014 study found **10 kinds of zooplankton**.

en: A "secret" lagoon that's **135 years old** and printed on every Golden Circle coach map. Some secret. It's the **oldest swimming pool in Iceland** — and the spot where the whole country first learned not to drown.

en: **Gamla Laugin** ("the Old Pool") at **Hverahólmi** by Flúðir was **built in 1891** — **Iceland's oldest surviving swimming pool**, older than the national grid, the republic, and your great-grandparents. The "Secret Lagoon" branding was bolted on 120-odd years later; the water never went anywhere.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: Before it was a pool it was a **parliament**: the local Flúðir assembly met on this exact patch until **1894**. Iceland's founding instinct, again — find a warm bit of ground and hold a vote on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: In **1909** it hosted **Iceland's first formal swimming lessons** — **32 men** in the debut course, girls following by **1911** — and taught the district every summer until **1947**. In a country ringed by a lethal North Atlantic, teaching the nation to swim in a hot bath was a genuinely brilliant life-hack.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin

en: Then it was **abandoned for nearly 70 years** — the village built a modern pool and left the old one to the algae. Scrubbed up and reborn on **7 June 2014**, history intact.

en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits the ground identified since **1841** as the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, held by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. **Ari fróði** put that þing on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, fourteen kilometres away, and nobody has ever closed the gap. en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village — a whole cluster of geothermal greenhouses (**Friðheimar, Espiflöt, Jarðarberjaland** — literally "strawberry land," and more). **Friðheimar** is the headliner: a working tomato greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Friðheimar / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: The crop drinks the volcano: **~95°C geothermal water** piped straight from a borehole heats the glasshouse, **LED grow-lights** fake a summer through the black winter, and the vines fruit **12 months a year — about 370 tonnes**, roughly **a tonne a day**, a serious slice of every Icelandic tomato. The same volcanic heat that warms Reykjavík's living rooms, just aimed at lunch.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Friðheimar / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: No native insect can pollinate a tomato flower this far north, so Friðheimar **flew in Dutch bumblebees** — a striped workforce knocking out **up to 2,000 flowers a day**. Iceland outsourced its pollination department to the Netherlands and never looked back.

en: Neighbour lake **Apavatn** ("Marsh Lake") is where the "cold politics" happened. In **spring 1238**, during the Sturlung Age, **Sturla Sighvatsson** (Sturlungar) ambushed and captured his rival **Gizur Þorvaldsson** (Haukdælir) right here — forcing him to swear on the Bible to give up power and sail to Norway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Geysir → Þingvellir / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: Gizur had his fingers crossed. He broke the oath, teamed up with **Kolbeinn ungi**, and five months later — **~1,700 men against ~1,000** — crushed the Sturlungar at **Örlygsstaðir (21 August 1238)**, the largest battle ever fought on Icelandic soil. Sturla's ancient family spear **Grásíða kept bending in his hands** as the tide turned; Gizur is said to have struck the fatal blow. So much for hot-tub diplomacy at the lake next door.

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm in **Meðalland**, right here in south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered out east to **Borgarfjörður eystri**; too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: The crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, the fishermen's union topped it up. **1911**: he tried **London** — the **Royal Academy slammed the door**. The rejection was the redirect: **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Home again, he painted Iceland like no-one had — knelt over the **moss and lava three inches from his nose**, and swore he saw **elves and hidden folk** in the cracks. (In Iceland, that's not a diagnosis. That's a career.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: In **1968** he handed the city a huge part of everything he owned — the museum's Kjarval collection runs to **thousands of works** — and he died **owning almost nothing.** The grey block in Klambratún is **Kjarvalsstaðir**, Iceland's **first purpose-built art museum** (1973); since **1995** his face is on the **2,000-króna note** — the only cod fisherman ever **promoted to legal tender.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Tómas didn't outrun Prohibition. He **outlived it** — on near-beer and a royal warrant.

en: **1913**: **Tómas Tómasson** starts Ölgerðin in a Reykjavík basement — at first just **malt extract** — and names it after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the Viking warrior-poet who could spin stunning verse and drink a whole hall under the table.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915). Wine creeps back in 1922, spirits in 1935 — but **beer stays illegal until 1989**. Why beer alone? It was seen as **Danish**, and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: So Ölgerðin cheats: brews **Egils Pilsner kept just under the legal 2.25%** — beer that technically wasn't beer. A loophole in a glass. (The orange **Appelsín** everyone drowns in malt at Christmas? That came later — **1955**.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The irony: Ölgerðin became a **purveyor to the Danish royal court** under King **Christian X** — a Danish royal warrant, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.

en: Just before the cones, that shallow lake on the right is **Rauðavatn**, “Red Water” — and the scruffy belt of trees beside it is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area**. In **1901** around eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake, and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first tried to ruin that joke.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / ⛰️ Rauðhólar

en: **Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was **viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru** — wooded from the mountains to the shore; today woodland covers about **1.5% of the country.** They dug **8,600 holes** here in **1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer — frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held (a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock **gengur þar inn og út**, in and out as they pleased). Only after the Second World War, with **close to 60,000 plants**, did it stick. The oldest **mountain pines** by the lake are now **over 100 years old** — a national repair job running since 1901.

en: The Cloud That Stopped Europe

en: In **2010**, this innocent-looking glacier volcano shut down **air travel for millions** who couldn't even say its name.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: **Eyjafjallajökull** — an **~800,000-year-old** stratovolcano, summit **1,651 m**, under an ice cap now shrunk to about **66 km²** — sits there looking like a tidy white lid over green fields.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: By volcanic standards **2010 was small: a VEI 4, only ~0.27 km³ of ash.** But it fired a **plume 8–9 km high** straight into the **jet stream** — and the glassy particles turn jet engines into **expensive sandblasters.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: Result: the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since WWII** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15–22 April**, about **48% of expected European traffic**, leaving roughly **10 million passengers unable to fly**, with airspace over some **20 countries** closed. Europe learned volcanoes don't read timetables.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: At farms like **Þorvaldseyri** right at its foot, **500–800 people were evacuated overnight** as meltwater poured off the ice; farmers **milked cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — then built a small visitor centre, because if a volcano rewrites your year you may as well sell the story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: Guest question, every time: does it trigger **Katla** next door? Historically the 920, 1612 and 1821 eruptions each were — but in **2010 Katla stayed shut.** Eyjafjallajökull is a **warning light, not a trigger.**

en: On **21 November 1973** a **US Navy Douglas C-117D** — a beefed-up "Super DC-3," though everyone insists on calling it a plain DC-3 — was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **both engines choked on carburettor ice over Vatnajökull.** Myth-bust: it did **not** "run out of fuel."

en: For decades a quiet local landmark; then **Justin Bieber** (2015) and the Bollywood hit *Dilwale* filmed here and **Instagram** did the rest. Today visitors walk a **4 km track each way** — the road was closed to cars in **2016** — across old ocean floor just to touch a wingless plane in a volcanic desert.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: **Pétursey** ("Peter's Island") is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock formed when a volcano **erupts under ice or sea** in the last Ice Age; hot magma met cold water, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**.

en: Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar sea stacks**, the last of an old headland where tough basalt held while the softer cliff was chewed away — the "stack" at the end of the crack-cave-arch-stack sequence. The cliffs above are a **puffin colony** in summer.

en: The biggest threat on the South Coast doesn't look like a threat — it's a **white ice cap, peaceful and silent**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Under that ice sits **Katla** — a **~10 km-wide caldera**, summit **1,512 m** — one of Iceland's biggest, angriest volcanoes. The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** — **520 km² as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890** — acting as a several-hundred-metre insulating blanket over a furnace.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: She's produced **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last one to come up through the ice, **1918**, ran **24 days** and dumped so much flood sediment — **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand** — that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: The gaps between her eruptions have run from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — and it is now **108 years since 1918, the longest quiet spell on record.** (Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Erupting under ice, she produces a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has drilled for this for decades.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Odd bragging rights: **Vík shares the title of Iceland's warmest weather station with Vestmannaeyjar** — around **5.9 °C** a year on the recent normals. en: Per *Landnámabók*, Hjörleifur settled here around **874** and, **within a year (c. 875)**, was **murdered by his own enslaved Irish/Hebridean men** — one of the very few slave revolts the sagas record. Ingólfur tracked them to the islands on the horizon and killed them in revenge.

en: Here's the payoff on the map: those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar** — the **"Isles of the West Men."** *Vestmenn* was the Norse word for the **Gaels of Ireland and the Hebrides** — so the archipelago out there is **named after the enslaved Gaels themselves.** The romantic image of free, self-made Viking farmers is missing a chapter.

en: At its base sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock." Every eruption, they say, is her ghost. **The volcano is named after her.**

en: The waterfall that **looks like a fantasy backdrop** and sounds like someone left a giant tap on **since the Ice Age**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: The **Skógá river** skips the rapids and walks straight off the old sea-cliff — a clean **60 m drop, 25 m wide** — free-falling into a deep pool before racing across the sandur to the Atlantic.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: At the base you have to **shout to be heard** — which is why most videos from here are people silently pointing. The metal staircase on the right is your free fitness test; at the top begins the **Fimmvörðuháls trail**, which climbs the river **between Eyjafjallajökull and Mýrdalsjökull** — the same gap the 2010 eruption first cracked open.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**: textbook waterfall geology — hard cap-rock over soft, undercut and collapsing, so the fall eats **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. The land then lifted, rivers dumped black sand, and the real shore marched several km south — Skógafoss never moved.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: Behind the car park: **Skógar Museum** (turf houses, old church, farm buildings) and a **bonus waterfall, Kvernufoss**, hiding in a green gorge next door. Plus the legend of **Þrasi's treasure** — a settler's gold chest hidden behind the falls; would-be looters snapped off the iron ring, which ended up on the **church door**. The gold did not follow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss

en: 🎬 **On screen:** The big one for filmmakers — *Thor: The Dark World* (2013), *Vikings* (Floki's storyline, Season 5), a *Game of Thrones* aerial sequence in the final season, the old *Beowulf & Grendel* (2005), India's *Dilwale*, *Aadhavan* and *Namo Venkatesa* — and yes, **Justin Bieber** clambered up it for his "I'll Show You" video.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Seljalandsfoss / 💧 Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi

en: A natural recess lets you walk **all the way behind the curtain** in summer — wet, slippery rock, so good boots, a waterproof and **one hand free**; in ice the path closes, so respect the barrier.

en: The cliff is an **old sea cliff from just after the Ice Age**, when the Atlantic reached the foot of the **Eyjafjöll**; rivers then filled the lowlands and the coast is now several km south — the same drowned-then-stranded coastline as Skógafoss down the road.

en: A short walk north, **Gljúfrabúi** ("the canyon-dweller") hides in a narrow mossy gorge — only its top peeks out; to meet it you **wade up the stream**, and **wet feet are non-negotiable.**

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **"Jói í Geitavík."** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

en: The whole valley was redesigned **~5,200 years ago** when **Leiti** erupted: lava poured down, hit the river and **split it in two**. Before, one river; after, two. Every waterfall here is the river's **5,000-year project** to saw back through solid basalt to the sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: The Elliðaá is one of the only **capital-city rivers on Earth with a wild Atlantic salmon run** — around **1,500–2,500** shove upstream past the joggers each summer. Reykjavík was so smitten it **bought the whole river in 1906.** (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: One kilometre of valley has hosted a **1750s wool mill**, a **drowning pool at Skötufoss** for women convicted of "moral crimes," outlaws in the lava tubes, **British WWII Quonset huts**, and a century-old hydro plant — **Elliðaárstöð (1921)**, the city's first, still humming.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur

en: Most Icelandically of all: a **1998 burst pipe** flooded the valley and, in a single weekend, **washed 10,000 years of buried history back into daylight.** Even the plumbing does archaeology here.

en: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system** — Hengill sits where **three volcanic and seismic zones meet**: the **Reykjanes rift**, the **Western Volcanic Zone** and the **South Iceland earthquake belt**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines. The white plumes are **steam**, not smoke.

en: After generating **303 MW** of electricity — plus half the capital region's hot water — the plant runs it **27 km** in insulated pipes to keep Reykjavík from reaching for a jumper.

en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, turning to **solid rock in a couple of years**. Next door, **Climeworks' "Mammoth"** fans (2024) suck CO₂ straight out of thin air and hand it to the same rock.

en: Hveragerði sits on the **Hengill system**, where **three volcanic and seismic zones meet** — the **Reykjanes rift**, the **Western Volcanic Zone** and the **South Iceland earthquake belt**. Geothermal *and* seismic at once, which is a rough combination for a postcode. Hot springs, steam vents and boiling mud pots break the surface **between the houses.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: On **29 May 2008** the ground threw a **doublet** — **Mw 5.8 beneath Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault about 5 km to the west**, the two starting **within 3 seconds of each other** for a **composite Mw 6.1** — and shook the town with ground acceleration up to **0.88 g** (near 1 g, the earth is shoving as hard as gravity). Rather than hide it, locals built the **Quake 2008** exhibition **on top of the fissure it opened**, crack left showing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Geothermal heat has been warming Icelandic greenhouses since **1924**, when the country's **first geothermally heated greenhouse** went up in **Mosfellssveit** — Hveragerði took the idea and made a living out of it, becoming Iceland's **market garden**: tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: And the famous **bananas**? Myth-bust: the college planted them ~**1950** as an *experiment*, output about **one tonne a year, never commercial.** Iceland is not, and never was, a banana republic. It's the most over-hyped tonne of fruit in Europe.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði

en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged it to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, announced that day as a **6.3**, epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. (Two quakes, one bang; nobody in town stopped to count.) And the best thing in **Sunnumörk** was never meant to be an exhibit at all: when the centre was under construction in **2003** an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at **over 6 on the Richter scale.**

en: One of the **shortest** rivers in Iceland — but it moves **more water than any other**. The final bottleneck for half the highlands.

en: Only **~25 km long**, yet **Iceland's largest river by discharge** — about **400 m³ every second**, draining a basin of **5,760 km²**. It's not the longest; it's the one you absolutely could not cross.

en: It's **four systems in disguise**. The glacial **Hvítá** — the silt-heavy water that thunders over **Gullfoss**, already fed by **Tungufljót** and **Brúará** — meets the clear spring **Sog** draining **Þingvallavatn**, and from Selfoss down they run as one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: It follows the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**, so the channel zig-zags along fault lines. Beside it sits **Þjórsárhraun**, about **8,700 years old**, roughly **1,000 km²** and **25 km³**, which ran **about 130 km to the sea** — the **largest lava flow on Earth since the end of the Ice Age** (Vísindavefur id=87471, Haraldur Sigurðsson, Jan 2025: *Þjórsárhraun er stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk*). (Most *powerful* eruption is a different trophy — that one goes to **Eldgjá in 939**.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Ölfusá

en: For centuries it was the **ultimate obstacle**: no bridge, just ferry crossings at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod**. When it flooded violently in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an "ice worm." It was a jökulhlaup. The monster version is the one that survived, because of course it did.

en: Per the saga, first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson** threw his carved **high-seat pillars** overboard and vowed to settle wherever they washed up. It took his slaves **three years** to find them — in a bay full of steam from hot springs, which he named **Reykjavík**, "Smoky Bay."

en: Myth-bust worth landing: he wasn't the **first** here. Irish monks (the **Papar**) were already in Iceland and left when the pagans arrived; a Norseman called **Náttfari** had stayed behind years earlier. Ingólfur's real title is narrower — **first *permanent* Norse settler in the saga tradition.** He got the trophy because his family later ran the parliament and wrote the record.

en: The town **only exists because of the bridge.** Before the **1891 Ölfusárbrú** — Iceland's first suspension bridge — the Ölfusá was uncrossable; once the bridge opened, trade clustered at the bridgehead and **Selfoss grew up around it.** The old construction hut, **Tryggvaskáli**, is still the town's oldest building.

en: In **WWII**, British troops guarded this crossing day and night — whoever held the only bridge over Iceland's biggest river held the south.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏗️ Selfoss

en: But in **September 1944** a milk truck tried to tow another broken-down milk truck across together. The **eastern cables couldn't take the concentrated weight, snapped, and both trucks dropped into the gorge.**

en: Both drivers survived — one clung to the **truck bed until he drifted ashore** by the church. The bridge was rebuilt in **five and a half months**, mid-war, reopening **21 December 1945** — the span still carrying you today.

en: Here's the twist: **the 2010 eruption was tiny** — only **~0.27 km³** of ash. But it punched an **8–9 km plume straight into the jet stream**, and the glassy particles turned jet engines into expensive sandblasters. A small volcano in exactly the wrong spot.

en: The first hit was local, not global: as meltwater poured off the ice, **500–800 people were evacuated overnight** from the farms below, and the ash fell thick enough to turn day into night.

en: At farms like **Þorvaldseyri** at its foot, people **milked cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — then built a visitor centre, because if a volcano rewrites your year you may as well sell the story back.

en: Then the global bill: the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since WWII** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15–22 April**, **48% of expected European traffic**, about **10 million passengers** who simply could not fly, and some **20 countries'** airspace closed. At the peak, **18–19 April**, that was roughly **19,000 cancellations a day**, and **US$1.7 bn** of airline revenue gone. en: Everyone calls it a "DC-3." It isn't. It's a **US Navy Super DC-3 (a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D)** — same family, buff cousin who went to the gym. It's worn the wrong name for fifty years like a stag-do lanyard.

en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying from **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors over the Vatnajökull ice cap** and both engines quit. The tourist story that it "ran out of fuel" is false — it iced up and became, in the co-pilot's words, "a massively overweight glider."

en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the shell.

en: **Dýrhólaey** was born underwater ~**100,000 years ago** in a submarine eruption — half tuff (**Háey**), half basalt (**Lágey**) — then hammered by waves into a huge natural **sea arch**. In **October 1993** a pilot flew a small plane clean through it **three times** (once could've been luck).

en: On top sits a **castle-like lighthouse** — Iceland's **first landfall light and brightest**, seen **43 km** out to sea; the current 1927 tower was designed by state architect **Guðjón Samúelsson** (yes — the same man behind that little church back down the road, and Hallgrímskirkja).

en: From the top you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. en: The name is literal: **Dýrhólaey** means **door-hill island** — the hill with the doorway through it. The first light went up here in **1910**; the tower you can see replaced it in 1927.

en: Under that ice sits **Katla**: a **caldera ~10 km across**, summit **1,512 m**, hidden beneath **Mýrdalsjökull** — **520 km² of ice as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890.** Being subglacial is the whole danger — she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: She's erupted **at least 21 times in the last 1,100 years**, with gaps running from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — usually bigger than her famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last eruption up through the ice — **1918** — lasted **24 days** and dumped **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand**, pushing **the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** The volcano literally added land.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: It is now **108 years since 1918 — the longest quiet spell on her record.** She even leaks CO₂ while dormant — one study put her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years. When this family goes big, it goes very big.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla

en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **221 m móberg cape** named after **Hjörleifur**, the **blood-brother** of Iceland's first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði

en: Around **875 CE** Hjörleifur forced his enslaved Irishmen to **drag his plough** like oxen; they killed his one ox, **blamed a bear** — and it worked, because Iceland *has no bears* and the newcomers didn't know that yet. When the men scattered to hunt the imaginary bear, the thralls murdered them and fled to the islands offshore. Ingólfur tracked them down and killed them; those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar**, the "Isles of the West Men," named for the very Irishmen who did the deed.

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **“Jói í Geitavík.”** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

en: Crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, the fishermen's union topped it up. **1911**: **London's Royal Academy slammed the door.** The rejection was the redirect — **1912** to **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Home again he painted Iceland knelt over the **moss and lava three inches from his nose**, swearing he saw **elves and hidden folk** in the cracks. (In Iceland, that's not a diagnosis — that's a career.)

en: **1914**: his **Bakkagerði** altarpiece shows Christ preaching from **Álfaborg**, the elf-rock, **Dyrfjöll** behind. The bishop refused to bless it — **too many elves, not enough Jesus** — so it still hangs there, gloriously **unconsecrated**. A second altarpiece, dismissed as “crude and ugly,” was bought by **Halldór Laxness** for **Gljúfrasteinn** (we pass it later). One man, two altarpieces, **zero bishops convinced.**

en: Founded **17 April 1913** by **Tómas Tómasson** in two basement bedrooms of a rented Reykjavík house — at first just **1%-alcohol malt extract** — and named for **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the warrior-poet who once rhymed his way off an executioner's block (the *Höfuðlausn*, “Head-Ransom”) and could drink a whole hall under the table. Aspirational branding.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915) — so Tómas sails to **Copenhagen and Germany (1915–17) to learn brewing anyway**, training up for a product his own country just outlawed. Wine creeps back in **1922**, spirits in **1935**, but **beer stays illegal until 1989** — because it read as **Danish**, and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The irony peaks in **1926**: after a state visit from King **Christian X**, Ölgerðin wins the right to style itself the **“royal brewery”** — a Danish royal blessing, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Real beer returned **1 March 1989** — now **Bjórdagurinn, “Beer Day.”** Egils didn't fight for shelf space; they already owned it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The field is the fresh top of the three-flow **Svínahraun** stack, radiocarbon-dated to around **1000 CE** — so it **inherited its name** from the conversion it coincided with. Fitting footnote: today the **CarbFix** project uses this very basalt to turn CO₂ into stone — the rock that once “proved” divine anger now mops up industrial emissions.

en: Hellisheiðarvirkjun
ctx: block title — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: While the world debates carbon capture, Iceland dissolves the problem in water, files it under “rocks,” and moves on.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system**, a rare **plate-boundary triple junction on dry land**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines — the white plumes are **steam**, not smoke. Built up in stages **2006–2011** to **303 MW**, it's **Iceland's largest geothermal power station**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: After the electricity, the leftover hot water runs **27 km** in insulated pipes to heat **more than half the capital region** — nothing wasted, and Reykjavík never has to reach for a jumper.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' “Mammoth”** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Iceland's largest geothermal power station, the steam plumes on your left
ctx: gloss for the name "Hellisheiðarvirkjun" — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Ölfusá
ctx: block title — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: Every drop that fell on the Golden Circle — glaciers, geysers, lakes — eventually squeezes through this one 25 km channel.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: One of the **shortest** rivers in Iceland — but it moves **more water than any other**. Four rivers in disguise, sharing a name only for the last **25 km**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: Only **~25 km long**, yet **Iceland's largest river by discharge** — about **400 m³ every second** off a **~5,760 km² basin**. Not the longest; just the one you absolutely could not cross.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: It's **four systems in one**. The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past **Gullfoss**, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará**; the spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's biggest natural lake. They meet just above **Selfoss** and from there run as one — the **Ölfusá**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: It follows the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**, zig-zagging along fault lines. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraun** — about **8,700 years** old, roughly **1,000 km²**, the **longest lava flow in Iceland**. Vísindavefur puts it higher than that (id=87471, Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025): *“Þjórsárhraun er stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk”* — the largest lava flow to have run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: For centuries the **ultimate obstacle**: unfordable, no bridge, just a ferry at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod** to reach the harbour at **Eyrarbakki**. When it flooded catastrophically in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an “ice worm.” (It was an **ice-jam flood**; the serpent just got the better press.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: That lava has a proper name and a frankly silly scale: **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava. It erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a **fissure 20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, well up in the interior, then ran **about 130 km to the sea**, reaching the coast **between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá.** Total volume: **25 cubic kilometres.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: On the magnitude scale Vísindavefur rates it **MS-9 — the largest Icelandic eruption by volume of erupted material** — ahead of **Eldgjá at MS-8** and a long way ahead of **Laki 1783 at MS-6.5.** That scale is logarithmic, so the gaps are wider than they look. Keep one distinction straight, though: largest by volume is not the same as **most powerful**, and that title goes to **Eldgjá**. The same system gave us **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477.** (The biggest eruption this island ever produced is shaped like a field. You cannot see it, and that is exactly how large it is.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: “Bridge-River”, one of the rivers the Hvítá gathers on the way
ctx: gloss for the name "Brúará" — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: “Tongue-River”, the other river the Hvítá gathers
ctx: gloss for the name "Tungufljót" — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá

en: Hveragerði
ctx: block title — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Pizza baked by a volcano, salad grown on steam, a museum built on an earthquake crack — all in the same town.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: A town of **about 3,350 people** (3,344 at the start of 2026) where the ground occasionally rearranges itself — so the locals **built an exhibition around the crack in their floor**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Hveragerði sits on a **three-way tectonic junction** on the edge of the **Hengill volcanic system** — geothermal *and* seismic, a rough combination for a postcode. Fumaroles and boiling mud pots vent **between the houses.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged it to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, **2008** — epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. It was a **doublet**: **Mw 5.8 beneath Ingólfsfjall** set off **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault about 5 km to the west** **within 3 seconds**, for a **composite Mw 6.1**. (Moment adds, magnitude doesn't — 5.8 plus 5.9 comes out at Mw 6.06. The **6.3** you will still see quoted was the figure announced in Iceland that same day, a teleseismic estimate.) It shook the town at up to **~0.88 g** (near 1 g: the earth shoving as hard as gravity), split buildings and re-plumbed the hot springs. (Two quakes, one bang; nobody in town stopped to count.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Cheap volcanic heat made it a **greenhouse town** from the 1920s (Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse** went up in **Mosfellssveit in 1924**) and Iceland's **market garden**: tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers — and, at the horticultural college, **experimental bananas** planted ~**1950**: about **a tonne a year, never commercial**. Iceland is *not* a banana republic — just the most over-hyped tonne of fruit in Europe.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today, 3,344 at the start of 2026** (Hagstofa MAN02005; the town passed 3,000 in 2023). The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Rather than hide it, the town put it on display — and the best thing in **Sunnumörk** was never meant to be an exhibit at all: when the centre was under construction in **2003** an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** That became **Skjálftinn 2008**, “The Quake” — stand on the crack, then ride the shaking simulator, which runs at **over 6 on the Richter scale.** **Admission is free**; you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hveragerði

en: Per the saga, **Ingólfur Arnarson** threw his carved **high-seat pillars** overboard and vowed to settle wherever they washed up. His slaves **Vífill and Karli** found them in a bay steaming with hot springs, which he named **Reykjavík**, “Bay of Smokes.” (The saga's “three-year search” wobbles even across the old sources — treat it as story, not stopwatch.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ingólfur Arnarson

en: Myth-bust: he wasn't the **first** here. Irish monks (the **Papar**) were already in Iceland and left when the pagans arrived; a Norseman, **Náttfari**, had stayed years earlier. Ingólfur's real title is narrower — **first *permanent* Norse settler in the saga tradition** — and he got the trophy because his family later ran the parliament and wrote the record.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ingólfur Arnarson

en: Selfoss
ctx: block title — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Selfoss

en: The town **only exists because of the bridge.** The **1891 Ölfusárbrú** — pushed through the Alþingi by MP and banker **Tryggvi Gunnarsson** — was Iceland's **first suspension bridge**; before it the Ölfusá was uncrossable, so trade clustered at the bridgehead and **Selfoss grew up around it.** The old construction hut, **Tryggvaskáli**, is still the town's oldest building.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Selfoss

en: Then in **September 1944**, after 53 years, a milk truck tried to tow a broken-down milk truck across at the same time. The **eastern bearing cables couldn't take the concentrated weight, snapped, and dropped both trucks into the gorge.** Both drivers survived — one clung to the **truck bed until he drifted ashore** by the church.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Selfoss

en: A replacement went up in about **five and a half months**, reopening **21 December 1945** — mid-war, because the town's lifeline doesn't wait, and that span still carries you today.

en: **Þjórsá** (“Bull River”) rises off the **Hofsjökull** ice cap and runs **230 km** to the sea — **Iceland's longest** — draining a **7,530 km²** catchment at roughly **383 m³/s**. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.

en: Those wide braided channels in the fields are **floodpaths**: when the glaciers melt fast, Þjórsá spreads across its plains rather than politely staying in one channel. Its valley, **Þjórsárdalur**, is farm country that neighbour **Hekla has buried more than once** in ash.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Þjórsá

en: It does **more electrical work than any river in Iceland**: **six power stations** on the Þjórsá–Tungnaá system (Búrfell first, **1969**) feed the grid — chiefly the **aluminium smelters** that are the reason a country of 380,000 makes so much power. en: Just after midnight on **23 January 1973** a **1.6 km fissure** tore open barely 200 m from town on **Heimaey**, and a brand-new volcano — **Eldfell**, “Fire Mountain” — began throwing lava through the eastern streets.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Skógafoss / Vestmannaeyjar

en: The lucky break was weather: a storm the day before had kept the **whole fishing fleet in harbour**, so of about **5,300 residents, roughly 5,000 were evacuated in around eight hours** — Iceland has **no army**, so the fishermen ran the evacuation themselves.

en: The eruption ran **five months** and buried about **400 buildings** — Iceland's own Pompeii, some houses now dug back out at the **Eldheimar museum**. To save the harbour, crews pumped **millions of litres of North Atlantic seawater** onto the advancing flow for weeks, and the cooled lava left the entrance **deeper and better sheltered than before.**

en: In front of you the **Markarfljót** runs **~100 km** to the sea off **two ice caps sitting on live volcanoes** — **Eyjafjallajökull** and **Mýrdalsjökull** — which is why it occasionally stops being a river and becomes a **jökulhlaup**. en: This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**: textbook waterfall geology — hard cap-rock over soft, undercut and collapsing, so the fall eats **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. en: Everyone calls it a “DC-3.” It isn't. It's a **US Navy Super DC-3 (a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D)** — same family, buff cousin who went to the gym. It's worn the wrong name for fifty years.

en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors over the Vatnajökull ice cap** and both engines quit. Myth-bust: it did **not** “run out of fuel” — it iced up and became, in the co-pilot's words, “a massively overweight glider.”
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / The DC-3 Wreck

en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the bare hull.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / The DC-3 Wreck

en: For decades a quiet local landmark; then a **Bieber video (2015)** and the Bollywood hit *Dilwale* filmed here, and Instagram did the rest. Cars were banned in **2016**, so now you walk a **4 km track each way** across old ocean floor to touch a plane with no wings. Not a joke in bad weather: the plain has **no shelter at all**, and **two visitors died of hypothermia** near the wreck in a January 2020 storm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / The DC-3 Wreck

en: A **275-metre lump of frozen explosion** — submarine volcano, one-time offshore island, saint's shrine, Sturlung-era fort, **WWII lookout post**, elf estate. **Most mountains never have a CV that long.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Pétursey

en: **Pétursey** (“Peter's Island”) is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock formed when a volcano **erupts under ice or sea**; hot magma met cold water, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Pétursey

en: For much of the Holocene the Atlantic really did surround it and sailors used it as a **landmark** — until **Katla**'s black sand slowly filled the gap and stranded it inland. Its old name literally meant **“Tall Island.”**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Pétursey

en: The name we use now comes from a **medieval shrine to Saint Peter** on the summit — a Catholic pilgrimage site before the Reformation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Pétursey

en: In the **Sturlungaöld** civil war, some **200 armed men fortified the summit** as a keep — **Þórðar saga kakala** records it as a refuge. In **WWII** the British reused that same 360° top as a lookout. The cliffs still host **fulmars and puffins**; the mound, inevitably, hosts **elves.** Two farms sit at the base: **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey.**

en: **Dýrhólaey** (“door-hill island”) was born underwater **100,000 years ago** in a submarine eruption — half tuff (**Háey**), half basalt (**Lágey**) — then waves hammered a huge natural **sea arch**, the “door” of the name, under **100 m cliffs.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Dýrhólaey

en: On top sits a castle-like lighthouse — **one of the most powerful lights on the coast** — first tower 1910, the concrete one **1927 by Guðjón Samúelsson**, same architect as the church a few stops back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Dýrhólaey

en: Long called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which held that title **for several decades** before the sea carried the sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back. In **October 1993** pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen** flew a light aircraft through the arch — three passes, to prove the first wasn't luck.

en: Black sand. A basalt pipe-organ. Sea stacks standing offshore. Iceland's most beautiful beach — and its most dangerous. Never turn your back on these waves.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar

en: ⚠️ **Safety first, always:** the "sneaker waves" (laumualda) here are lethal and unpredictable — they surge far higher up the beach than the sea in front of you suggests, the water is freezing, and the undertow drags. People have drowned here, several in recent years. Stay well back, keep off the wet sand, and never turn your back on the ocean for a photo.

en: The cliff is stuðlaberg — hexagonal basalt columns formed as thick lava cooled slowly and cracked into near-perfect pillars; the Hálsanefshellir cave folds them into a natural pipe-organ you can walk into when the tide allows.

en: Most countries' founding stories are statues and speeches. Iceland's is a body, a fake bear — and a woman who became a volcano.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

en: **Hjörleifshöfði** — a **221 m móberg headland** — is named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two **sailed here together around 874**, then split: Ingólfur let the gods choose his home, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík; Hjörleifur — who **refused to sacrifice to any god** — parked at the first headland. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

en: Come spring, says *Landnámabók*: **one ox** — so his **enslaved Irishmen dragged the plough**. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears** — the newcomers just didn't know that yet. When the Norsemen scattered to hunt it, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, then fled with the women and boats to the islands offshore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

en: Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers to those islands, and killed them all. His eulogy: **“A sad end for a good man, slain by slaves — that's what comes of refusing to sacrifice.”** Those islands became the **Vestmannaeyjar** — **“Isles of the West Men,”** the Norse name for **Irish Gaels** — **named after the enslaved men who did the deed.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

en: The ghost came **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **magic breeches that never tired**. Shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. When sinking whey threatened to expose the body, she fled onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and **leapt into the chasm still called Kötlugjá — “Katla's rift”** — the volcano's vent. Soon after, a **glacial flood burst from the ice**. **The volcano is named after her** — and every eruption, they say, is her temper.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

en: Like Pétursey, this cape **was once an island** — tethered to Iceland by miles of Katla's black sand.

en: **Laufskálavarða** is a low **lava ridge on the east edge of Mýrdalssandur**, by the river **Kúðafljót** — carpeted in **stone cairns.** The custom: anyone crossing this deadly black desert **for the first time** piled a cairn for a **safe journey**, and centuries of first-timers built the field you see.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: The danger was real — **Mýrdalssandur is Katla's flood path**, swept by **jökulhlaups** without warning, so a little supernatural insurance made sense.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: The name comes from **Laufskálar**, a big settlement-era farm here — tradition gives it **24 doors on iron hinges** — buried by **an early Katla eruption.** (You'll see a “894” date on the signs; the maths doesn't work, so just call it an early Katla eruption.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Laufskálavarða

en: Don't add to it: visitors are now **asked not to build new cairns** — the field is protected heritage, not a DIY project.

en: One fissure, one very bad year, a whole continent's weather rearranged. The prettiest thing out here is also the deadliest.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: Every other lava field is scenery. This one has a body count.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The Fires of 1783
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: That soft green moss you can't stop photographing? It's the lid on the **deadliest eruption in Iceland's history** — the one that nearly ended the country.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: In **June 1783** the **Lakagígar** fissure tore open — a **27 km rift of more than 140 vents** — and erupted for **eight months** (the **Skaftáreldar**, “Skaftá Fires”), laying down **14.7 km³ of lava across ~600 km².** That makes it **the second-largest lava flood in historical time, behind Eldgjá** and its **~20 km³** — larger still, but **8,700 years before anyone was here to see it**, is **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**. You're driving across the runner-up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: And yet the lava barely killed anyone — the **gas** did. The fissure breathed out **~122 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide** plus a fluorine fog that poisoned the grass, and the famine that followed has a name of its own: the **Móðuharðindin, “Mist Hardships.”** The haze even crossed **Europe**, wrecking harvests as far as France.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The green fuzz is **grámosi**, woolly fringe moss — **decades to grow, one boot-print to wreck.** Admire it through the window.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The **Skaftáreldar** began on **8 June 1783** and did not stop until **7 February 1784** — eight months to the day, near enough.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: It did not spread politely across country, it went down the rivers: on **11 June** the **Skaftá** simply stopped, and on **3 August** the **Hverfisfljót** went the same way. Two rivers deleted, by something arriving down their own beds.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: Landgræðslan measures that moss mat at an average **38 centimetres** thick, which is also why nothing else grows here — **well over two centuries on**, vascular plants are still sparse, because the mat smothers seeds before they germinate.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The arithmetic of the **Móðuharðindin**: roughly **10,000 dead — about a fifth of all Icelanders** — the population down from just under **50,000** to just under **40,000** by the end of **1786**, with **smallpox** taking another **1,500** and **earthquakes in August 1784** flattening about **400 farms**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The haze formed a continuous cloud across the whole northern hemisphere, **30 to 90 degrees of latitude**, depositing **over a tonne of sulphuric acid per square kilometre**. Europe called it the dry fog and spent that summer wondering where it came from.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: The national figure hides the local one. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** puts the livestock loss at **around three quarters of every animal in the country** — and in the worst-hit districts, the ones we have just driven through, **about 40% of the people died.** (One in five is the headline. Out here it was two in five.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun

en: A village so holy that, by legend, **sinners literally couldn't live here** — and then in 1783 a priest stared down a wall of lava and won.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Tradition (via *Landnámabók*) says the **Papar** — Irish monks — were here **before the Norse**, and the ground was so blessed no heathen could settle. In **1186** the Benedictines made it official: **Kirkjubæjar convent**, a nunnery that ran until the **Reformation in 1550.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: The place-names still gossip about the nuns: **Systrafoss** (“the sisters' falls”), lake **Systravatn**, and **Systrastapi** — the rock where, the darker tale goes, two sisters were burned for sin and only later cleared.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Nearby is **Kirkjugólf**, the “church floor”: a patch of **columnar basalt** worn flat so it looks like a tiled cathedral floor. Nobody laid it — **the volcano did the tiling.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: And this is where **Rev. Jón Steingrímsson** delivered his **Eldmessa — the “Fire Sermon” — on 20 July 1783**, preaching as the Laki lava bore down. It halted at the edge of the parish. He kept preaching.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: The convent was founded by **Þorlákur helgi**, Bishop of Skálholt and later Iceland's patron saint, and its first abbess was **Halldóra**, about whom the record says almost nothing at all.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Behind the two-sisters legend sits one documented case: in **1343** a nun of this house — the sources cannot agree whether **Katrín or Kristín** — was **burned at the stake** for heresy and for having given herself to the devil in writing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: She is an outlier twice over. Iceland's actual burning age was the **17th century** — the **first burning for witchcraft** was **1625** and the last **1685** — and of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned about **23** were for witchcraft and the overwhelming majority were **men**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: **Kirkjugólf** is not weathered flat, it is decapitated — *jökul- og brimsorfið stuðlaberg*, columns planed off by a glacier and scoured by the sea. Protected **náttúruvætti since 1987**, with a **10-metre** exclusion zone and a **50-metre** buffer, so walk to it and do not stand on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: **Séra Jón Steingrímsson**, **1728–1791**, is the **eldklerkur**, the fire priest, and the reason we know any of this in detail — he wrote the eruption down almost day by day. He also buried a great many of the parish he had held together, once the famine arrived.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Kirkjubæjarklaustur

en: Two footnotes the story usually loses. The charges against the nun in **1343** were not only heresy and having given herself to the devil in writing — she was also accused of having **misused the body of Christ.** And what the ground shows at the Fire Sermon is a lava front that **stalled**, held up by the terrain and by its own cooling crust. Both things are true at once, and Icelanders have never felt any pressing need to choose between them.

en: **Fjaðrárgljúfur** (“feather-river canyon”) is **about 1.5 km long and up to 100 m deep** — those are the figures in its own protection order — a snaking gorge with mossy green **palagonite (móberg)** walls.

en: Two ages, don't mix them up: the **rock is about 2 million years old** (Ice-Age palagonite), but the **cutting began about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age**, when meltwater from a retreating glacier sawed straight down through the soft rock — **and it is still going on today.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: The **Fjaðrá** river still does the digging, one grain at a time. That serpentine shape is just water taking the lazy route — and turning it into art.
