en: In **2015 Justin Bieber** filmed *I'll Show You* wading through it; Instagram did the rest. So many boots trampled the moss that the site now **closes periodically to recover.** Two million years of rock, nearly worn flat by one music video.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: 🎬 **On screen:** this snaking canyon also stars in the *Game of Thrones* dragon-flight sequence (Season 8, Episode 1, just before the Skógafoss landing).

en: It is not finished. The protection notice states plainly that the cutting **is still ongoing**, and **100 metres** in **10,000 years** works out at roughly **a centimetre a year** — a hundred metres of rock removed at about the rate your fingernails grow.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: “Closes periodically” has hard dates. It shut in **February 2019** for waterlogged ground and reopened **31 May 2019**; then the notice went out on **5 April 2023** and the gate shut the next morning, at **09:00 on 6 April 2023**, under the emergency power in **Article 25a of the Nature Conservation Act no. 60/2013**, reopening **20 April 2023** after two weeks of gravel being carried in and laid. That gravel is what you are standing on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: It was finally protected on **11 May 2024** by **Auglýsing nr. 555/2024**, covering **0.15 km²** — **fifteen hectares**. A patch you could walk across in ten minutes needed a legal instrument of its own.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Fjaðrárgljúfur

en: And the closures work: after the 2019 one, **Umhverfisstofnun** recorded that the vegetation had taken **remarkably well** to being left alone — which is the whole argument for the path, in one sentence.

en: **Orustuhóll** (“battle hill”) is a **rock knoll** that, before **1783**, sat as an island in the **floodplain of the Hverfisfljót river**, ringed by water and sand.

en: When the **Skaftáreldar** (the Laki fires) sent the **Eldhraun / Brunahraun** lava pouring east, the flow **split around the hill and left it standing** — a green survivor-islet in a sea of fresh black rock.

en: So it's a rare thing: a scrap of the **pre-1783 landscape** you can still see, marooned inside the lava — and the district around it was emptied. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** counts **twenty estates buried outright and thirty more wrecked**; **Vísindavefur** counts **thirteen farmsteads under the lava and twenty-nine holdings abandoned**. en: That wall is **Lómagnúpur**, and it comes up before the sandur does: **Núpsstaður at route km 263.1, Lómagnúpur at 265.5**, both on the **left, north of the road**, while **Skeiðarársandur proper does not begin until km 268.6.** In **chapter 133 of Brennu-Njáls saga** the cliff swings open like a door and a man in a goatskin cloak walks out with an iron staff, names **Flosi's** men one by one, calls himself **Járngrímur**, and says he is bound for the **Alþingi** to clear the juries, then the courts, then the battlefield.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður

en: The dream at **Lómagnúpur** is a death list, read out in order. **Járngrímur** names **Grímur the Red**, **Árni Kolsson**, **Eyjólfur Bölverksson**, **Ljótur son of Hallur of Síða**, the **Sigfússynir**, then **Lambi**, **Móðólfur** and **Glúmur**, and last of all **Gunnar Lambason** and **Kolur Þorsteinsson.** Flosi had been shaken awake at **Svínafell** by **Glúmur Hildisson** and told the whole thing to **Ketill úr Mörk** — whose reading took one word, *feigir*, doomed, and whose advice took one sentence. Tell nobody.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður

en: Tucked under that cliff at **Núpsstaður** is a **bænhús**, a one-farm prayer house — a timber box **6.15 by 2.50 metres** inside a turf shell, **no pulpit, no font, unpainted throughout**, church dated **1657** and the standing timber to about **1850**. It has been in the care of **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands since 1930.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Lómagnúpur & Núpsstaður

en: The paperwork on the **Núpsstaður bænhús** is the best of it. **Minjastofnun** lists it as a **friðlýst kirkja** with the designer recorded, with admirable Icelandic honesty, as **Ókunnur** — unknown. The turf shell is **about 9 m long and 7.5 m wide**; side walls and the back of the chancel are **stacked turf and stone up to window height**, and the roof is **krossreist** and laid with turf. Inside: a **flagstone floor** in the nave with a bench along each wall, a chancel raised **two steps**, an altar under a small window, and **no altar rail.**

en: **Skeiðarársandur** runs to **about 760 km² on Náttúrufræðistofnun's register — one of the great sandur plains anywhere**: black sand and braided rivers, dumped grain by grain by the glaciers pouring off **Vatnajökull.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: For centuries this was **the gap in the ring**: unbridgeable rivers that could flood without warning. The **Ring Road (Route 1) wasn't finished until 1974**, when the Skeiðará bridge finally welded the country into one loop.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Then on **4 November 1996** the **Gjálp/Grímsvötn** eruption melted the ice cap and loosed a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood — peaking near **40,000–50,000 m³ a second, briefly rivalling the Amazon.** It **tore a 24-metre section out of Skeiðarárbrú**, twisting steel girders like wire.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Those **mangled girders now stand as a roadside monument** — Iceland's polite way of saying “we rebuilt it, but don't get comfortable.”
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: The piece that closed the loop was **Skeiðarárbrú**, started **1972** and finished in **July 1974** at **904 metres** — the **longest bridge in Iceland**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: For scale on **1996**: the **Ölfusá at Selfoss** averages **400 cubic metres a second**, so the flood was running at roughly **125 times** that, carrying icebergs the size of vans. Total damage came in around **1.5 billion krónur** at 2007 prices.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Rebuilding was quick and quietly humiliating: the span went back up at **880 metres** instead of **904**, and in **2017** it was retired altogether — the national record went backwards to **Borgarfjarðarbrúin at 520 metres**, because the river the big one was built for wandered off. (A national record trimmed by a river that could not be bothered to use the bridge.)

en: To your left is an ice cap so big it makes **its own weather**, hides **live volcanoes**, and covers **roughly 7% of the entire country.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: **Vatnajökull** is **Europe's largest ice cap by volume** — around **3,000 km³ of ice**, up to **~1,000 m thick**, over **about 7,500 km² by 2023 on Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður's own figure** — the last hard measured inventory, **Jökull 70**, put it at **7,720 km² in 2019.** Either way, **roughly seven percent of the country, and shrinking.** Beneath it sit active volcanoes like Grímsvötn and Bárðarbunga — fire under a very thick lid.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: Poking up at **Öræfajökull** is **Hvannadalshnúkur, 2,110 m — Iceland's highest point.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: 🎬 **On screen:** Svínafellsjökull — the glacier tongue here — is a Hollywood regular: the League of Shadows' ice-training in *Batman Begins* (2005) and the frozen "Mann's planet" in Christopher Nolan's *Interstellar* (2014) were both shot on this very ice.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: Tucked into the green oasis of **Skaftafell** is **Svartifoss**, a waterfall framed by black **basalt columns** — the very shape that inspired Reykjavík's Hallgrímskirkja. It's a national park (2008) and **UNESCO World Heritage site (2019).**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: The measured sequence for **Vatnajökull itself** is brutal: **8,723 km² around 1890**, **8,087 km² in 2000**, **7,745 km² in 2014**. And for **all of Iceland's glaciers together** — not just this one — the cover has gone from **12% of the country 130 years ago to about 10% by 2014**, thinning by roughly **a metre a year.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: Icelandic research puts the endpoint plainly — on current trends the country's glaciers will be **largely gone within two centuries**. The tongues along this road have already pulled back **around 4 kilometres** since measurements began in the **1930s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: **Öræfajökull** in **1362** produced the **largest explosive eruption in Iceland's recorded history** — about **10 cubic kilometres** of tephra, ash on roughly **75%** of the country, **30 to 40 centimetres** deep locally, out of a caldera of **about 12 km²**. It has erupted once since, in **1727**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: Before **1362** the glacier was **Knappafellsjökull** and the district was **Litla-Hérað**, the Little District. Both names were abandoned: **öræfi** meant a harbourless coast and came to mean wasteland, and the survivors renamed their own home **The Wasteland**, where it has stayed for **664 years**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: **Svínafell**, at the foot of that film-star tongue, is where **Flosi Þórðarson** was sleeping badly when he dreamt the mountain opened — the same man who led the burning of **Njáll**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

en: The 1362 eruption did not merely bury Öræfi — it ran over it, with **pyroclastic flows sweeping out across the lowland** as the ash came down. And note where the summit sits: **Hvannadalshnúkur stands on the rim of that ice-filled caldera.** Öræfajökull is not a mountain with a volcano in it. It is a **volcano with a mountain on it.**

en: **Fjallsárlón** is Jökulsárlón's **smaller, quieter sibling** — a meltwater lagoon at the snout of **Fjallsjökull**, an outlet glacier tumbling off **Öræfajökull**, Iceland's highest volcano.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón / Fjallsárlón

en: Because it's tighter and less famous, you stand **much closer to the glacier wall** — the ice front looms right across the water and calves chunks into the lagoon with a crack like a rifle shot.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón / Fjallsárlón

en: The icebergs here are **smaller but packed tighter**, streaked with **black volcanic ash** and that impossible **blue** — the colour of ice so compressed the air has been squeezed clean out of it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón / Fjallsárlón

en: No armada of tour boats, no crowds — just the glacier, the bergs, and **Öræfajökull** brooding behind. Like its big sister, this lagoon **didn't exist a century ago**; it's a product of the retreat.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón / Fjallsárlón

en: **Ari Ólafsson**, physicist at the **University of Iceland**, gives the mechanism: in water and ice the **red** end of the spectrum fades far faster than the **blue**, and in clear dense ice daylight travels **tens of metres** through a block before it comes back out, losing red, yellow and green on the way. The white ones are white because cracks and air bubbles scatter the light straight back out before anything can be absorbed — same ice, different amount of air.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fjallsárlón / Fjallsárlón

en: Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður dates the whole family in five words: *"Lón tóku að myndast upp úr 1930"* — **the lagoons began forming after 1930**, as the ice pulled back off the sand. There are three big ones — **Fjallsárlón**, **Breiðárlón** and **Jökulsárlón** — the same story at three different scales, and this is the one still sitting **closest to its glacier front.** (The famous one has had time to run away from its own ice. This one hasn't.)

en: This lagoon is **Iceland's deepest lake** — and it **didn't exist** when your great-grandparents were born.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: **Jökulsárlón** (“glacial-river lagoon”) only appeared around **1934–35**, when the glacier **Breiðamerkurjökull** began retreating and left a hollow that filled with meltwater. It's now **the deepest lake in Iceland — the published figure is 260 metres, and it is still deepening as the glacier retreats.** About **25 km²**, and it has **quadrupled since the 1970s.** You are looking at climate change with a boat tour on it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: The **icebergs** calving off the glacier can be **centuries old** — glowing blue, streaked with black ash from past eruptions, drifting for years before they melt. Floating archives.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: It's **tidal**: a short channel links it to the sea, so the water is **brackish** and **seals** cruise in to hunt herring. Watch for heads bobbing up between the bergs.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: Hollywood noticed — **two James Bond films, Batman Begins and Lara Croft** were all shot on this ice.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: The bottom of it is **the lowest point in Iceland** — *lægsti staður landsins* — reaching far below sea level. Not a valley and not a cave: a hole a glacier dug and then walked out of.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: For the runners-up: **Öskjuvatn** manages **220 metres**, **Hvalvatn 160**, and **Þingvallavatn** — the one on everybody's postcards — a mere **114**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: **Breiðamerkurjökull** has pulled back **about 7 kilometres** here against **around 4** for the other Vatnajökull tongues, and the reason is the lake itself — brackish water now sits against the ice front and melts it. The glacier is being eaten by its own runoff.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: That salt is also why **it never sets**: even in a hard winter the surface of the lagoon does not freeze solid.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Jökulsárlón / Jökulsárlón

en: When bergs in Jökulsárlón finally shrink small enough, they **float out the short Jökulsá river to the sea** — and the **tide flings them straight back** onto this black volcanic beach, **Fellsfjara** (part of **Breiðamerkursandur**).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: Stranded on the black sand, the clear and blue ice glitters like **scattered diamonds** — hence the nickname. Every piece is **ancient glacier**, salt-polished and melting in front of you.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: Because it's **tidal**, the beach **restocks itself every few hours** — no two visits match, and a berg you photograph now may be gone by afternoon.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: One serious note: **never turn your back on the surf here.** The **Jökulsá river mouth has vicious currents and sneaker waves** — beautiful, and genuinely dangerous. Admire the ice; respect the water.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: Every block out there is **old compressed glacier ice**, not frozen seawater — it was inside **Vatnajökull** for a very long time before turning up at your feet for ninety seconds of fame.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: The names here are ancient and descriptive — **Breiðá**, **Breiðamerkursandur**, **Jökulsá** — and then there is **Diamond Beach**, which is English, recent and coined for visitors. It went through a very public argument in Iceland in **July 2019** about whether tourism was quietly renaming the coastline.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: This sand is named after a farm. There was settlement on **Breiðamerkursandur** from about **1100 years ago**, and then the **Little Ice Age** — **Breiðamerkurjökull** advanced furthest in the **18th and 19th centuries** and at its maximum the ice front got to **within about 250 metres of the open sea**, taking everything in its path underneath it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara / Fellsfjara

en: Look right at 2 o'clock — Mýrdalsjökull, and Katla under it.
ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: We've said her name half a dozen times today — under Sólheimajökull, off Dýrhólaey, at the church on the hill, in the cairn field, on Hjörleifshöfði. **Here's the volcano itself.** And the biggest threat on the South Coast doesn't look like a threat — it's a **white ice cap, peaceful and silent.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Under that ice sits **Katla** — a **~10 km-wide caldera**, summit **1,512 m** — one of Iceland's biggest, angriest volcanoes. The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** — **520 km² as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890** — a **200–700 m** insulating blanket over a furnace. Being subglacial is the whole danger: she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: She's produced **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: The gaps between her eruptions have run from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — and it is now **108 years since 1918, the longest quiet spell on record.** (Do that sum on the bus and watch the faces.) She also leaks so much CO₂ while dormant that one study ranked her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Erupting under ice, she makes a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has drilled for this for decades.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Her last full eruption began shortly before **3pm on 12 October 1918** and ran until **4 November** — twenty-four days — and the flood carried roughly **200 million cubic metres** of rock and ice to the sea, a cube **585 metres** on every side. It dumped so much sediment that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: The ash of **1918** came to about **0.7 cubic kilometres** spread over **60,000 km²**, more than half the country, with the plume reaching **at least 14,300 metres** and the finest dust above **25 kilometres**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Nobody died in **1918**, and the Icelandic record is blunt about why — *"sennilega olli tilviljun"*, probably just coincidence. The flood came down where nobody happened to be standing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Her system's **Eldgjá** was not a day but a campaign: it **began in the spring of 939 and ran on, at least episodically, into the autumn of 940**, along a fissure **75 kilometres** long, and that flow ran **about 70 kilometres** to the sea. Vísindavefur rates it **VEI-6** — similar to **Laki** in lava volume, **about 20 km³ against Laki's 14.7** — but **a full magnitude and a half above it on the MS scale**, which is why Vísindavefur calls Eldgjá **the most powerful Icelandic eruption of the last ten thousand years.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: **VEI-6** is rare company. Across the whole of the last **10,000 years** only a handful of Icelandic eruptions have climbed that high — the **Saksunarvatn** tephra event of about ten thousand years ago, **Veiðivötn in 1477**, and this one. Vísindavefur puts Eldgjá **about 840 years before the Lakagígar eruption of 1783.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: The whole belt between **Mýrdalsjökull** and **Vatnajökull** is built out of these — the remains of **fissure eruptions tens of kilometres long**, some from the ice age and some from after it. **Lakagígar, Eldgjá, Veiðivötn, Vatnaöldur.** Four names, four gashes, one neighbourhood. And Vísindavefur states plainly that **another great fissure eruption in this belt is all but certain** — in the system of **Grímsvötn**, **Katla** or **Bárðarbunga** — and that it could come very soon or in many centuries. (Nobody will tell you which, which is the least reassuring answer available.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / Katla

en: Iceland's **southernmost mainland village** — about **300 people** in the village, **~750** in the wider district — strung along the beach with **Víkurkirkja** parked safely up on the hill. With **no natural harbour**, this was historically a place you rowed boats out through the surf from an open shore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: It's also, **jointly with Vestmannaeyjar**, the **warmest place in Iceland** (**5.3°C** yearly mean) — Veðurstofa's own wording is *ásamt Vestmannaeyjakaupstað*. And it is properly wet, about triple Reykjavík. “Warmest” is doing heroic work in that sentence.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: That shore we just talked about — the one **1918** shoved out past **Hjörleifshöfði** — is this town's front garden: everything out there is fresh Katla sand.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: To the east, **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once sat by open sea — is now stranded **inland**, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black sand. The church above town is the official “**run here if Katla wakes**” point.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: The weather station here was set up in **1925** and has observed continuously ever since. **Veðurstofa Íslands** gives the annual mean as **2,333 mm** over the standard period **1971 to 2000** — a lot of rain, but not a national record: Iceland's wettest year anywhere is **Kvísker, 4,630.4 mm in 2002.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: The wettest year on record is **1926 at 2,887 mm** — the station's second year of operation, which must have felt like a discouraging start. **1950** and **1959** are barely behind at **2,858** and **2,855 mm**, and the heaviest single day is **150.3 mm on 9 September 1933**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: The temperature extremes are **28.5°C on 11 August 1939**, which the Met Office itself marks as **doubtful**, and **minus 16.9°C on the night of 1 April 1968**, which nobody has ever queried.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: None of that exists without **Guðný Helgadóttir**, who has been observing the weather at Vík **since 1972** — one person, one place, decades of readings taken by hand in whatever was falling that morning.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Vík / Vík í Mýrdal

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm, **Meðalland** — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri** — the fjord still calls him **"Jói í Geitavík."** Too poor for paint: **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then to sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: In **1968** he handed the city a huge part of everything he owned — the museum's **Kjarval collection runs to thousands of works** — and the country's most valuable artist died **owning almost nothing.** That grey block in Klambratún is **Kjarvalsstaðir**, Iceland's **first purpose-built art museum** (1973); since **1995** his face is on the **2,000-króna note** — the only cod fisherman ever **promoted to legal tender.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval

en: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. The original ran right here — set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⚖️ Kjalarnes

en: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — the first settler's son — held the **Kjalarnesþing** before Þingvellir's famous **930**. **Ari fróði** is the only near-contemporary source and he puts it right here: *"en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi"*. Tradition then has him **consecrating** the big one. Build the prototype, bless the franchise. **The snag: no assembly has ever been found on Kjalarnes.** **Jónas Hallgrímsson** examined **Leiðvöllur** here in **1841** and called it a footpath; the national register still lists it *sést ekki* — nothing to see. The ruins he did find were **fourteen kilometres away at Þingnes on Elliðavatn**, protected since **1930** as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*, and the join between the two has **never been proven**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⚖️ Kjalarnes

en: Laws? They sent one man — **Úlfljótr** — to Norway for **three years** to copy the **Gulating law**. He came home with Iceland's first law code, minus one feature: **the king**. Stole the software, deleted the boss.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⚖️ Kjalarnes

en: Bonus first, same ness: Iceland's **earliest recorded church** — built by an Irishman around **900**, a century before we officially converted. Archaeologists dug: old buildings, **no church**. The paperwork outlived the building. Very relatable.

en: The numbers, because they're the whole show down here: **5,770 metres long** — roughly **63 blue whales stacked nose-to-tail**, because Iceland loves its whales — and **3,750 of them run under the sea**. Deepest point: **165 metres below sea level**, with up to **40 metres of water** over the roof. If you're claustrophobic, just pretend you're in a very damp IKEA car park.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Blasting started from both ends in 1996, the crews met in the middle, and it opened *ahead of schedule* on **11 July 1998** — the same year *Titanic* won Best Picture. Coincidence? Probably. Cost: **4,630 million krónur** at 1996 prices… or one slightly used volcano.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Before the tunnel, driving round the fjord took **an hour**. Now: about **7 minutes** — enough time to recite the Icelandic alphabet (*good luck*), explain why Björk's swan dress was *art*, and question your life choices as you descend into literal darkness. One single tube, by the way — because why build two when you can play chicken with oncoming traffic?
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

en: Designed for 5,000 vehicles a day; now about **8,800** use it like a drive-thru for fermented shark, and the toll went in **2018**. There's serious talk of a second tube — imagine two straws in a milkshake, but the milkshake is made of basalt.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🕳️ Hvalfjörður Tunnel

ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The folklore — filed as folklore, from Jón Árnason's collection: a man refused to acknowledge his child by an elf-woman, and was turned into an evil whale with a red head — **Rauðhöfði**. He smashed **nineteen boats** before two priests conjured him up the fjord — thereafter **Hvalfjörður** — and into the lake above — thereafter **Hvalvatn**. Whale bones "are said" to have been found up there. *Said.*
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The waterfall he was forced up: **Glymur**, named for the din. **198 metres**, long held to be Iceland's highest — a rival was measured taller in 2011, never confirmed. Glymur is contesting the ruling.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The island: **Geirshólmi**. Harðar saga puts **180 outlaws** on it, until the local farmers lured them ashore and killed them at **Þyrilsnes** — dated **986**. Hörður's wife **Helga** swam for it with her two boys; the sound is still called **Helgusund**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: The digging: **1881**, an archaeologist opens the grave-mound — *"nothing there."* The island: **no trace of any building**. A hundred and eighty men, zero evidence. The honest version — and the better story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: Then the 20th century: from **1940** the fjord hid Allied convoys — and Geirshólmi, island of outlaws, spent the war as a **gunnery target**. Aggro level: maximum. Postcard-serenity: also maximum. Very Hvalfjörður.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / 🐋 Hvalfjörður

en: Twelve to thirteen thousand years ago, in the **Bølling** warm spell, the land was still pressed flat under the weight of the ice sheet and the sea stood correspondingly high — high enough to cut a **wave-cut notch into Akrafjall at 105–125 metres** above today's sea level. And a **whale bone has been found at 85 metres** up the mountain. That's a beach line and its residents, parked the height of a church spire above the modern shore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: Same rock as Esja: the lavas here erupted between about **4.5 and 3 million years ago**, one continuous basalt sheet with the mountain across the water — until glaciers cut **Hvalfjörður out of the middle of it, 2.5–3 million years ago**. Esja and Akrafjall aren't neighbours; they're the two halves of the sandwich the ice ate.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: Hidden bonus: the **Gilbert/Gauss magnetic reversal** — the Earth's field flipping over, **3.6 million years ago** — is recorded in the mountain at about **350 metres elevation**. A compass error, archived in basalt.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: The people: written tradition — Landnámabók, so tradition, not archaeology — says that shortly after **880** two brothers came **from Ireland**: **Þormóður and Ketill, sons of Bresi**, Irish-born, Norwegian descent. They claimed all of Akranes and drove out the family already living there. Þormóður farmed at **Innri-Hólmur**, the last farm before the tunnel; where Ketill settled, the sources disagree — even Akranes's own town history says "uncertain." A thousand years on, and we still haven't sorted the brothers' addresses.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Borgarnes / ⛰️ Akrafjall

en: The clue they left is in the names: **Akranes, Akrafjall, Akrakot, Garðar** — a cluster of grain-field place names, cited as evidence the Irish brothers actually grew corn here. The map remembers the harvest.

en: Under the water: the whole Borgarfjörður lowland was once sea floor — the flats around here are **marine sand and clay** lying between basalt knolls. You're bridging a fjord that's mostly given up being one.

en: The town in the saga is **Digranes**. **Skallagrímur** — Egill's father — took the land "between mountain and shore," named his farm **Borg** and the fjord **Borgarfjörður**; his man **Grani** got the land at Digranes and built **Granastaðir** — which, by the local reading, makes Grani's household the first inhabitants of what is now Borgarnes. Skallagrímur's own farm, **Borg á Mýrum**, is still there — church and farm, visible north-west of town. A settlement claim you can check from the car park.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Kveldúlfur's coffin.** Egill's grandfather died at sea on the voyage out — and ordered his crew to put him overboard *in a coffin*, telling his son to settle wherever it washed ashore. They later found the cove where the coffin landed, carried it onto the ness, and piled stones over it. Local tradition points at **Kveldúlfshöfði**, just south of town — with the honest hedge that it's "not fully clear" where the coffin actually beached. Either way: this family's estate agent was a dead man in a floating box.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Brák.** Skallagrímur, mid-berserk rage during a ball game, seized the boy Egill — and the woman who stepped in was Egill's foster-mother, **Þorgerður brák**. He chased her to the outer end of Digranes; she leapt from the cliff and swam for it; he hurled a great stone that struck her between the shoulders, "and neither came up again." The sound below the old town is still called **Brákarsund**. A servant woman, drowned a thousand years ago — and her name is on the water and half the street signs. Iceland picks its heroes carefully.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: The town itself, in one breath: first house built **1857** by a Scot called **James Ritchie** — no relation, probably — for canning salmon; trading licence **1867** after 212 locals signed the petition. Population when Ritchie arrived: effectively zero. Now: the saga capital of the west.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: **Skallagrímur's mound.** When his turn came, his body was taken out through a **hole broken in the house wall**, rowed out at high tide, and buried on the point of the ness **with his horse, his weapons and his smith's tools**. Years later Egill reopened the mound and laid his drowned son **Böðvar** beside him — the scene in the 1970 bronze relief in **Skallagrímsgarður**, two minutes' walk from here. The mound is a protected monument. It has been dug into, more than once. **Nothing — no bones, no artefacts — has ever been found in it.** That's the honest version, and it's a better story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes / 🪦 Borgarnes

en: If the graves whet the appetite: the **Settlement Centre** down by the harbour opened on **13 May 2006** and tells this exact saga. And one closing twist — **Snorri Sturluson**, the man widely believed to have *written* Egils saga, married the heiress of Borg and lived there from **1201**. The suspected author, living on the story's home farm. Write what you know.

en: Why does this peninsula have volcanoes at all? The plate boundary **left six million years ago** — packed up, moved to Reykjanes — and Snæfellsnes **kept erupting anyway**. Most recently in the **10th century**. Some things don't take the hint.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: The whole ridge ahead is **Iceland's first rift zone** — the original crack, running through Snæfellsnes and north into Húnaflói. It stopped rifting about **6 million years ago**, and the spreading jumped south-east to **Reykjanes**, where all the recent fireworks are.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: And then the peninsula ignored its own retirement. Volcanism restarted, and today Snæfellsnes carries **three volcanic systems**: **Ljósufjöll** in the east, little **Lýsuskarð** in the middle (**30 km by 5** — the runt of the litter), and **Snæfellsjökull** at the tip.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Iceland's First Rift Zone

en: The eastern system is a rebel twice over: nearly every Icelandic volcanic system runs SW–NE, but this one runs **SE–NW** — at right angles to the active rift's fissures. (Iceland's spatial planning, ladies and gentlemen.)

en: The **Ljósufjöll system** runs nearly **90 km** WNW–ESE, and its lavas have travelled **at least 15 km** from the mountains — as far as the mouth of Hvammsfjörður on the far side. One system, most of the horizon.

en: The ridge itself is mostly **móberg** — hyaloclastite. During ice ages it erupted *under* the glacier and built ridges of consolidated volcanic glass; between ice ages the lavas ran down the valleys. Same volcano, two completely different products, depending on whether there was a lid on.

en: Some of it is uncomfortably fresh: **Hólmshraun** in Hítardalur may have flowed **shortly before the settlement**, and its dated neighbours run about **2,600** and **3,600 years old**. In geology terms, the paint's still wet.

en: Now the history. **1148**, Hítardalur, up that valley on the right: Bishop **Magnús Einarsson** of Skálholt was at a feast when the building burned. The annals put the toll at **roughly eighty people**, the bishop among them — the deadliest fire in Icelandic history, and it happened at dinner.

en: **Eldborg** is an oval crater, about **200 m long and 50 m deep**, sitting mid-lava **38 km north of Borgarnes**. It's the textbook shape for this system: eruptions here open on a short fissure, then focus down into one big dome-shaped crater. The fissure is the draft; the crater is the final edit.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🌋 Eldborg

en: The Environment Agency records **two eruptions** here — the later one "most likely during the Settlement Age." That's the official wording, and we'll keep it: the honest answer to "when exactly?" is that nobody's published a firm date. Possibly the first settlers got a show.

en: Its lava, **Eldborgarhraun**, covers about **32 km²**, and the crater rim reaches **100 m above sea level** — with birch woodland around the base, which is rarer in a lava field than you'd hope.

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Nobody carved these columns. Cooling rock shrinks, shrinking rock cracks, and the hexagon wins because it's the roundest shape that still fills a plane with no gaps.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: It's the same maths as a beehive. The bees do it in wax in a summer; the basalt did it in stone over years — and neither of them ever took a geometry class.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Nobody Carved This
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Who stacked all those pillars? Nobody. That wall on the right did it to itself — and the reason it's **hexagons** is the same reason bees build hexagons: **geometry only offers so many options**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: **Gerðuberg** is a belt of columnar basalt — *stuðlaberg* — running between two farms, with the slopes below it coming right down to the road. The columns look quarried, dressed, and stacked by a contractor with a level. They weren't. No hands involved.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: Here's the mechanism, properly: basaltic melt is fully **solid at about 1,000 °C** — but it's still cooling after that, and cooling rock **contracts**. Shrinking solid rock has to crack. The cracks organise into columns, usually **six-sided**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: And they're hexagons because the hexagon is the shape **closest to a circle that still tiles a plane with no gaps**. Triangles and squares tile but aren't remotely circular; octagons are nicely round but leave gaps. The hexagon is the compromise candidate — and in geology, as in politics, the compromise candidate wins.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: The columns always grow **perpendicular to the cooling surface** — and up close they carry horizontal "chisel marks," **1–2 cm** per groove, each one a record of a single cracking increment. The rock kept its own worksheet.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: For a sense of the timescale: on Heimaey, a **40-metre-thick** lava took about **ten years** to cool and crack all the way through. A wall like this wasn't built in a day; it wasn't even *cooled* in a decade.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: As for how tall Gerðuberg is exactly — I'd love to give you a number, but there's no official measurement published, and on this bus we don't invent figures, we just point at the wall.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / 🪨 Gerðuberg

en: The road under you is exactly as old as **Wikipedia** — both launched in **2001** — and the flat-topped mountains beside it were built **under an ice sheet**. Brand-new tarmac, Ice Age scenery, no middle ground.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: **Road 56 — Vatnaleið**, "the lakes route" — is nearly the newest thing you'll touch today. The transport minister cut the ribbon on **Friday 2 November 2001**, standing down at Selvallavatn where we're headed, and the old **Kerlingarskarð** pass was retired that same day after generations of hauling traffic over the peninsula's spine. **16.4 km** of new road, topping out at **230 m** against Kerlingarskarð's **311 m** — and only **3 km** of it above 200 metres, where the old road had **ten**. We replaced the pass, not the mountains.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: Those flat-topped mountains flanking the road are **móberg** — the same fought-a-glacier-and-lost rock from this morning's drive, now on both sides of you. The whole spine of Snæfellsnes is built of it, and the ice sheet that made it left ten thousand years ago. Never came back for its work.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Borgarnes → Selvallafoss / ⛰️ Vatnaleið

en: Icelandic farmers named **everything**. Seventy-nine separate features on this one abandoned farm — every gully, every boulder, the rock where the hidden people sang. They did not name the waterfall. And the name on your map today? Somebody in tourism made it up.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: Start with the river, because the internet gets this wrong constantly. This is **Fossá** — literally *"waterfall river."* It is **not** Straumfjarðará. Straumfjarðará rises in Baulárvallavatn, back the way we came, and runs the opposite direction to the sea at Straumfjörður. Different river, different catchment, different ocean-facing coast.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: **Landmælingar Íslands**, the National Land Survey, has this fall in its database. Mapped, plotted, classified as *foss*. The name field is **blank**. Náttúrufræðistofnun holds the same point, also blank.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: So I went looking. **Zero** hits for "Selvallafoss" in Árnastofnun's national place-name archive. **Zero** in the national mapping database — the only "Selval-" name in the whole country is the lake. **Zero** across the entire Icelandic newspaper corpus, which runs back well over two hundred years. "Selvallavatn" gets 71 hits. The waterfall gets none.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: Meanwhile the place-name survey of the farm above us lists **Steinkarl**, **Nóngjá**, **Krummaklettar**, **Stóriklettur** — *"where the hidden people sang."* Seventy-nine names. They named a rock for its singing elves and left the waterfall alone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: I think the old answer was just simpler than ours: the river was **already** called *the waterfall river*. Naming the waterfall on the waterfall river is like opening a restaurant called Restaurant.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: And no — **nobody has ever officially measured its height.** No figure in the national survey, none in the natural history institute, none in *Íslenskir fossar*, the standard reference on Icelandic waterfalls, which records two other falls in this district and skips this one. Every number you'll find online was typed by somebody with a website and a deadline. I'd rather give you nothing than give you a number I can't stand behind.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 💧 Fossá

en: One last thing while we're demolishing: **sel** does not mean sheep, and it does not mean seal. A *sel* is a **shieling** — the summer dairy station where the milking animals went up the valley. **Selvellir** means *"the shieling flats."* In the **1700s** the farm Horn was split in two, and the new half was built on Horn's old shieling ground. The farm went empty in the **1920s** and never came back.

en: Water pours into this lake all day long. **Nothing flows out of it.** Not a stream, not a trickle, nothing above ground. Somewhere under that lava the whole lake is quietly draining away — and nobody has ever proved where it goes.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: **Selvallavatn** sits at **62 metres** above sea level in a hollow between Berserkjahraun and the mountain wall. Fossá runs in on the east, small becks run in on the south. And that is the entire hydrological story, because there is **no outflow above ground.** None.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: The man who wrote down the place-names here was **Lárus Halldórsson**, born on the farm above us in **1920**. Going back over the survey he added a feature the earlier recorder had missed: **Rás** — a swallow-hole at the lava's edge *"where the water is sucked in a whirlpool down into the lava."* Then he added one careful sentence: **perhaps that is the answer to the riddle of Selvallavatn's outflow.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: *Perhaps.* He left it open. And as far as I can find, in the eighty-odd years since, **nobody has closed it.** No dye trace, no survey, no paper. A lake disappearing into a lava field, and the last word on it is a farmer's son saying "maybe."
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: It hasn't always been Selvallavatn either. The old name in the record is **Svínavatn** — *pig lake.* Less romantic, and it clearly lost the marketing meeting.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: There's **brown trout and Arctic charr** in it — the trout run a solid **three to six pounds**, and on summer evenings shoals of small charr work along the lava edge. In a dry spell the water level can drop by **a metre and a half**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: How big is it? Genuinely nobody agrees. The standard Icelandic reference says **0.85 km²**. The national mapping database maps the shoreline at **0.30 km²**. That is a factor of nearly three, on a lake you can see the whole of from here, and I am not going to pretend I can settle it. **Maximum depth: never surveyed at all.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss / 🌀 Selvallavatn

en: How do you get rid of eighteen ghosts? Iceland's answer, year 1000: **take them to court.** Charges, pleadings, verdicts — and closing statements from the defendants.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: *Eyrbyggja saga*, chapters 50 to 55 — and it starts in the harbour we just left: the year **1000**, a ship from **Dublin** wind-bound **at Rif**. Aboard: **Þórgunna**, a Hebridean woman near sixty — tall, dark-browed, formidable — with bedding finer than anything Iceland had seen.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: **Þuríður**, mistress of the farm **Fróðá** here — "greedy for finery and a great one for show," the saga's words, not mine — tried to buy the lot. Þórgunna's answer: **"I will not lie in straw for your sake."** So Þuríður moved her in and played the long game.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: Þórgunna sickened and died. Her deathbed instruction was precise: **burn the bedding. All of it.** The husband burned the mattress and pillow — and kept the treasures. One act of greed, and the saga invoices everything that follows to it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: Then Fróðá came apart: a **seal's head rose out of the fire-pit** — out of the *fire* — staring at the hangings that should have burned, and every club-blow drove it **higher**. Drowned men walked into their **own funeral feast**, soaking wet. Of **thirty** in the household, **eighteen died** and five fled.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: And the ending is *us*: **Snorri goði** sent a priest, yes — but the real remedy was a **door-court**. Every revenant formally **summoned, charged, tried and sentenced** at the door of the house. Each ghost rose as its verdict fell — Þórir wood-leg: **"We have sat while sitting could be borne."**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 👻 Fróðá

en: They burned the canopy, the priest sang the offices, the hauntings stopped — and Kjartan lived long at Fróðá and became "the greatest of champions." They didn't exorcise the ghosts. **They sued them.** And won.

en: The kicker: around **1960** the harbour went *back* — Rif rebuilt as the district's main fishing harbour, 270-odd years after the river ruined it. Geography took three centuries to change its mind. It never apologises.

en: Killed on This Spot, 1467
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: What's more dangerous than being the richest man in Iceland? **Standing between English merchants and their cod.** In 1467, right here, the King of Denmark's own governor found out.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: **Björn Þorleifsson the Rich** — head of the Skarð family, one of the wealthiest houses in Iceland — sailed for Copenhagen in **1456**, got seized by Scots at Orkney on the way, and came out of the whole mess ennobled: **King Christian I** gave him a coat of arms — a **white bear on a blue field** — and made him ***hirðstjóri***, governor of Iceland, **for life**. "For life" turned out to be the operative clause.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: In **1466** the king banned the English from trading in Iceland. The English ignored him — they had a trading post here and cod is cod. In **1467**, English merchants killed Björn at Rif. What he was doing here, nobody wrote down; later sources say his son had been seized and he came to free him. His death sat inside a real Anglo-Danish trade war, settled by treaty in **1473**. Icelandic historians file the whole era under *Ten Cod Wars, 1415–1976* — this was an early round.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: Now the folklore layer, and I'll label it: the **axe-mark on Björnssteinn**, the body **cut in seven pieces and sent to his widow in barrels**, and her answer — **"Do not weep for farmer Björn — gather men instead."** Every one of those details was **first written down more than a century after the event**, in the late 1500s, with what the scholars politely call a strong folk-tale colouring. The record gives us one line; folklore wrote the screenplay.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: His widow, **Ólöf the Rich Loftsdóttir**, needs no embroidery anyway: the king's own letter to the King of France calls her *mulier spectabilis* — "a distinguished woman." Royal correspondence rated her before the barrels ever entered the story.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🪓 Björn the Rich

en: And a footnote for the pedants (I am one): even the **information sign at the stone** gets the war wrong — its five-year war ending in 1474 doesn't stand up. Trust the stone; check the sign.

en: This wetland holds **17,000 nests** of arctic tern — the **biggest single colony in Iceland**, by a distance, and big enough to qualify as **internationally important**. For scale: the runner-up colonies on this peninsula are Arnarstapi at **850** nests and Kvíabryggja at **500**. That's not first place. That's a different league.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / 🐦 The Tern Capital

en: The commute: some of these birds winter at the **edge of Antarctica** and fly here to breed — pole-ish to pole-ish, twice a year, every year, on a wingspan you could cover with a tea towel.

en: By **12 August** the breeding season is mostly done — which is the only reason we can stand this close in peace. en: **Hellissandur** is reckoned **one of the oldest fishing stations in Iceland** — no founding year, because no source will stand behind one, and we don't invent dates on this bus. Named for the shore cave **Bennuhellir**, where the catch was processed.

en: On the hill: **Ingjaldshóll**. Church built **1903** — one of Iceland's oldest concrete churches — with tradition claiming the site back to the early 1300s. Also the farm where **Eggert Ólafsson** grew up, where the **1754 glacier climb** set out. Told you the name would come back.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / ⛪ Hellissandur, Ingjaldshóll & the Columbus Story

en: The story you may have read: "Columbus wintered at Ingjaldshóll in 1477." What Columbus actually left us: one note — in February 1477 he sailed **"one hundred leagues beyond" Thule**. That's it. **He never said he went ashore**, and Iceland's own record is silent.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ólafsvík → Djúpalónssandur / ⛪ Hellissandur, Ingjaldshóll & the Columbus Story

en: Where the wintering story really comes from: **fiction** — a short story by the Danish author **Sophus Bauditz**, serialised in the emigrant paper *Heimskringla* in **Winnipeg from 1889**, then translated "back" into Icelandic. One scholar's verdict, and it's the phrase to keep: **"fiction historicized."** The parish-hall painting (1998) is a 20th-century picture of a 19th-century short story.

en: The saga gives Bárður a CV like no other settler's: his father **Dumbur** was descended from **giants**, with **troll stock** in the line; his mother **Mjöll** was human. Half-troll, half-giant, part human — the saga is genuinely specific about the mix, and so are we.

en: From age ten he was fostered by **Dofri**, a *bergbúi* — a mountain-dweller, a being that lives *in* the mountain — who taught him genealogy, fighting skill, and "magic and ancient lore." At thirteen he married Dofri's daughter. A conventional childhood, by the standards of nobody.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Djúpalónssandur → Arnarstapi / 🛁 Bárðarlaug

en: Arriving on Snæfellsnes, says the saga, he came to a pond, took off all his clothes and **washed at its edge** — and the pond is called **Bárðarlaug**, "Bárður's bath," to this day. He built his farm just there: **Laugarbrekka**, "bath slope." The man named half the neighbourhood after one wash.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Djúpalónssandur → Arnarstapi / 🛁 Bárðarlaug

en: Now the precision point, and I love this: *laug* means a warm pool — but the official management plan for the site states there has been **no geothermal heat in that pool since the settlement of Iceland**. So whatever Bárður did here, **he did it cold**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Djúpalónssandur → Arnarstapi / 🛁 Bárðarlaug

en: What the pond actually is: an oval pool in a **scoria crater planed down by a glacier** at the end of the Ice Age, protected as a natural monument since **1980** — invisible from the road, invisible until you stand on the rim. A bath with privacy walls, courtesy of the last glaciation.

en: This coast is a working census: the columns record how the lava cooled, and the nests record what the ocean is doing right now — and the second number is moving fast.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: About ten thousand pairs of kittiwakes nest along this coast — nearly two per cent of the Icelandic population. And they fell by fifty-five per cent in one year, between 2017 and 2018.

en: Columns Lying Down on the Job
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: Basalt columns are supposed to stand up straight. Half of the ones on this coast are **lying flat on their sides** — and the rock is following the rules by doing it.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: The clefts along this shore are the **Stapagjár** — columnar basalt, *stuðlaberg*, running **both vertical and horizontal**. Same maths as Gerðuberg this morning — columns grow perpendicular to whatever cooled them — except half of these cooled sideways. Read the angle and the rock tells you which way the heat left.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: The ledges hold about **10,000 pairs of kittiwakes** — just under **2% of Iceland's entire population** of the species — plus roughly **12,500 pairs of arctic terns**. Now the hard number: kittiwakes here **fell 55% in one year**, 2017 to 2018. Not "declining somewhat." Fifty-five per cent. Someone counted the nests, twice.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: While you're walking, look **out**, not just down: **orcas, harbour porpoises and minke whales** are regularly seen off this coast. No promises — they haven't read the itinerary.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🐦 The Arnarstapi Cliffs

en: Housekeeping: **45 minutes** here, and the **cliff path is the whole show** — statue, clefts, bird ledges, harbour. **Toilets are here**, so use them; the next stretch of road is lava, and lava is not discreet.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: That statue is six metres high and close to three hundred tonnes of stone, unveiled on the seventeenth of June 1985 — and it is not only a saga monument: the family who commissioned it raised it in memory of their parents and a brother who died of exposure.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: The Detail Almost Every Guide Misses
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: Six metres of stacked stone, close to **300 tonnes** — a saga giant guarding the harbour. And the detail few guides know: it's also **a family's gravestone**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: The figure is **Bárður Snæfellsás**, by the sculptor **Ragnar Kjartansson**, unveiled **17 June 1985** — about **6 metres high** and using **close to 300 tonnes of stone**. You don't move that; you build it where it stands and let it outlast you.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: You met him at Bárðarlaug an hour ago — here's his ending: he vanished **into the glacier**, and the saga says people **"believed in him almost throughout the peninsula"** and made vows to him. His title, *ás*, is the same word used of the old gods. A vow-god, not a mascot.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: Now the part that changes how you look at it: the statue was **commissioned by the children of Jón Sigurðsson of Bjarg á Stapa and Guðrún Sigtryggsdóttir, as a memorial to their parents and their brother Trausti — who died of exposure young**. A saga giant on the outside; a family remembering the weather's cost on the inside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🗿 The Bárður Statue

en: And Arnarstapi itself is in the saga: *"Þorkell rauðfeldur took land for himself at the place called Arnarstapi."* You are standing in a named sentence from the Middle Ages.

en: Empires file paperwork; harbours do the work. The monopoly, the governor and his house are all gone — the landing they came for is still landing fish.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: This was a monopoly-trade harbour and the seat of the district governor. His house was built here in the 1770s and 80s — and then dismantled and shipped away in 1849.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: Flat-Packed in 1849
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: This little cove was once the **seat of government for western Iceland**. Then somebody took the government building apart, put it on a boat, and **shipped it away**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: Arnarstapi was one of the harbours of the **Danish monopoly trade** — the *einokunarverslun* — and the landing here was reckoned **one of the best "under the Glacier."** Where the trade sat, power sat: this became the residence of the **amtmaður**, the district governor.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: The house itself went up **1774–87**, built by the Royal Trading Company for its trade manager **Hans Hjaltalín** — one of the very few Icelanders ever to hold such a post under the monopoly. Trade was freed in **1787**, he bought the business and the house; he went bankrupt around **1820**; and from **1821** it housed the governor of the West Amt. One building, three careers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: Then the move: in **1849–50** the house was **taken down and carried away by sea** to Vogur á Mýrum — and moved *again* around 1983, to Korpúlfsstaðir, for storage. (We don't demolish good timber. We forward it.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: What's left is what matters now: the small-boat harbour, **rebuilt in 2002**, is today **the only harbour on the whole south side of Snæfellsnes** — motorboats since about 1933, and it still fishes year-round. The governor left; the fish didn't.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi / 🏠 The Governor's House That Left

en: A gorge and a sea-crag, each named for the boy who died there — ages eleven and twelve, one under each arm. Icelandic place names are the country's oldest court record.

en: The saga is very precise about the two boys: eleven and twelve years old. Bárður carried one under each arm up the mountain — and the gorge and the crag ahead of you both still carry their names.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: One Under Each Arm
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: Bárður again — and this time it's not a bath. Two boys, aged **eleven and twelve**. He took them **one under each arm**, walked up the mountain — and the gorge and the sea-crag where it ended **still carry their names**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: The setup: the children were playing on the ice, there was a quarrel, and it ended with Bárður's daughter **Helga** adrift on an ice floe — the saga floats her all the way to Greenland in seven days. Bárður came back "very dark of countenance." The saga's phrase, and it's doing a lot of work.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: The boys were **Rauðfeldur and Sölvi**, sons of the neighbour Þorkell at Arnarstapi — **one was eleven winters old, the other twelve**. The saga is precise about the ages, so we are too. Bárður took them both, one under each arm, and walked up the mountain.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: **Rauðfeldur** he threw into a gorge "so deep that he was dead the moment he came down" — **Rauðfeldsgjá**, the black cleft at three o'clock. **Sölvi** he carried further and threw over a high sea-crag — **Sölvahamar**, on the coast ahead. A thousand years on, the map still files both boys exactly where they landed.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: Precision point, because guides get this wrong daily: the saga **never names Stapafell**. It says only "up the mountain." The pyramid ahead certainly looks the part — but the text doesn't put Bárður on it, and we don't put words in a saga's mouth.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛰️ Stapafell & Rauðfeldsgjá

en: What Stapafell actually is: a **526 m pyramid of móberg** — same under-the-ice recipe as the Ljósufjöll ridges this morning — summit called Fellskross. As for the gorge, no official geological survey of it exists — so the only authority on Rauðfeldsgjá's origin is, for now, the saga. Make of that what you will.

en: In a country famously short of murderers, one farm on this coast produced the national serial killer — nine confessed, eighteen alleged, one execution, three graves.
ctx: the point of the block — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: Nine confessed. Some say eighteen. Buried in 1596, in three separate pieces — because when Iceland finally gets a villain, we take absolutely no chances with the sequel.
ctx: the spoken close — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: The Farmer You Didn't Stop To Visit
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: Iceland has, in its entire recorded history, essentially **one serial killer**. One. He farmed on **this coast** — and the travellers who crossed his path had a habit of **not continuing their journey**.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: His name was **Björn**, of the farm **Öxl** — which is why history files him as **Axlar-Björn**, "Björn of Öxl." His victims were **travellers**: people passing through this district, exactly the way we are now, minus the upholstery.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: When it ended, he **confessed to murdering nine** of them — and some accounts say **eighteen**. We quote the confession, and we flag the higher figure for what it is: an account, not a count.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: The bodies, it was said, went into the pond **Iglutjörn**. "It was said" is doing honest work in that sentence — that's how the record itself puts it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / 🔪 Axlar-Björn

en: He was **executed in 1596**, and the authorities took no chances with the afterlife logistics: he was **buried in three parts**, at Laugarholt near Hellnar, just along our road. Sixteenth-century Iceland's version of absolutely-definitely-finished.

en: The Widow Who Rebuilt the Church
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: How does a small parish on a lava field get its church back? One widow. **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** filed the paperwork with the church authorities, put up her own money, and **rebuilt it herself** — and the black church on that lava is hers.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: The black church is **Búðakirkja**. First church on the site: **1703**, built by Bent Lárusson. The one you're looking at is the widow's: **Steinunn Sveinsdóttir** applied to the church authorities for permission, then led and paid for the rebuild herself — **rebuilt in the late 1840s, consecrated in 1851**. (The archives offer three build dates; the consecration is solid, so that's the one we stand on.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: Legend has it Bent Lárusson appeared to Steinunn **in a dream** and asked her to do it. That's the story as recorded — told as legend, kept as legend. She died a few years later and lies in this churchyard, gravestone still standing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: The church has been **legally protected since 1 January 1990**, was moved within the churchyard in one piece in **1984**, and today belongs to the National Museum. A museum piece that still holds services — Iceland doesn't really do "retired," see also: this entire peninsula.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: Under it, **Búðahraun**: lava from the **88 m** crater Búðaklettur, about **5,000–8,000 years old**, and its beach sand is **nearly pure olivine** — the lava carries yellow-green olivine crystals, and the sea has milled the rock down to its minerals. Green-gold sand, next to a black church.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: The lava is also the county's botanical garden: **over 130 plant species**, including **11 of Iceland's 16 fern species**, in a nature reserve since **1977**. Somebody counted the ferns. Eleven. They're probably still out there, counting.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Arnarstapi → Ytri-Tunga / ⛪ Búðir

en: **03 · Ísland farsælda frón** — *Karlakór Reykjavíkur*. The melody Icelanders actually sing is the wrong one. Helgi Helgason's tune gets the credit — but the version everyone knows is centuries older, a Lydian-mode chant from medieval manuscripts that got married to Jónas Hallgrímsson's 1835 lyric long after the wedding bells. A 600-year-old tune wearing 19th-century words.

en: **06 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.

en: **10 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.

en: **11 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **12 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **13 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **14 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **15 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **16 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **17 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **18 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **19 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg

en: **20 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]

en: **21 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]

en: **22 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.

en: **23 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.

en: **24 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.

en: **25 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.

en: **26 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.

I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.

en: The pale flats are **Löngufjörur** — "the Long Beaches" — running from Hítarnes in the east all the way west to Búðir. The sand is **pale-yellow shell sand**, ground-up seashells, flat as far as the eye can see and almost without a stone. Note the colour; in a country famous for black beaches, we're driving past a blond one.
